All normalizations and the logarithm have nonzero positive denominators or arguments under the stated hypotheses.
notes.TorusEuler.PaperLimitAgreement: For specified approximate velocities $U_j$, a time $T$ and fields $u,p$, the formal condition requires a smooth odd periodic Euler solution on $[0,T)$ and smooth odd divergence-free initial data. It requires $U_j(0)\to u(0)$ in every spatial $C^{m,1/2}$ norm, and $U_j\to u$ in those norms uniformly on $[0,S]$ for every $S<T$. It also requires a continuous velocity on the closed slab and uniform velocity convergence through $T$. Every maximal solution from $u(0)$ must have lifespan at least $T$ and agree before $T$. These conditions strengthen the introduction’s $C^m$ convergence claim. The spatial norm sums the supremum and one-half Hölder seminorm of derivatives through order $m$.
notes.TorusEuler.PaperMeanIntegratedSolution: On $[0,T]$, a solution here consists of a continuous curve $v$ of weakly divergence-free $C^{0,1/2}(\mathbb T^3)$ fields and a fixed divergence-free field $c$, satisfying $\mathbb P(Kv-J(\Omega v)+L)=c$ and $Jv(T)=0$. Since $Jv(0)=0$, its displacement has both zero endpoint values. The half-Hölder norm is the maximum of the supremum and seminorm. This is the projected form of (4.9); it does not yet supply a scalar pressure or prove existence. All asserted equations concern the designated interval, despite the functions being defined for every real time. Here $Jw(t)=\int_0^tw(s)\,ds$.
notes.TorusEuler.PaperMeanIntegratedSolution.c: Suppose a continuous divergence-free half-Hölder velocity $v$ satisfies $\mathbb P(Kv-J(\Omega v)+L)=c$ on $[0,T]$, with $T\ge0$, $K(0)=I$ and $L(0)=0$. Then $c=v(0)$, since the primitive vanishes at zero and the Leray projection fixes $v(0)$. These are the initial conditions used in §4.3 for a source obtained by integrating a force. The additional identification $c=b(0)$ uses the actual flow normalization $X_{0,0}=I$ and $D_aX_{0,0}=I$; it is not part of this algebraic conclusion. Here $Jw(t)=\int_0^tw(s)\,ds$.
notes.TorusEuler.PaperMeanIntegratedSolution.e: Let $T\ge0$, and let divergence-free $z,v,c$ be half-Hölder fields with continuous $v$, $z_t=v$ on $[0,T]$, and $z(0)=z(T)=0$. Suppose $Kv-J(\Omega v)+L=c+G$, where $G$ is the gradient of a differentiable periodic potential at each time. Then the same $v,c$ solve the projected endpoint equation and $z=Jv$ throughout the interval. This is a conversion of an already supplied solution, not an existence theorem for a prescribed source. Periodicity is essential for the Leray projection to remove the gradient. Here $Jw(t)=\int_0^tw(s)\,ds$.

Let $K,\Omega,L$ be time-continuous half-Hölder fields on $[0,T]\times\mathbb T^3$. Suppose continuous divergence-free $v$ and constant $c$ satisfy $\mathbb P(Kv-J(\Omega v)+L)=c$ and $Jv(T)=0$. Then there is a periodic potential $\phi(t,\cdot)$ of zero spatial mean whose gradient $G$ is continuous in time in $C^{0,1/2}$ and satisfies $Kv-J(\Omega v)+L=c+G$. Mean zero is integration over the unit torus. This recovers the pressure gradient in (4.9). The conclusion does not assert time differentiability of the scalar potential. Here $Jw(t)=\int_0^tw(s)\,ds$.
notes.TorusEuler.PaperMeanIntegratedSolution.p: Suppose two integrated equations on $[0,T]$ use the same coefficients and source, their velocities agree on this interval, and their time-independent fields agree. If their remaining terms are $G_1$ and $G_2$, so that $Kv-J(\Omega v)+L=c+G_i$, then $G_1=G_2$ throughout $[0,T]$. This is the final algebraic step in pressure-gradient uniqueness for Theorems 4.2 and A.1. It assumes velocity uniqueness rather than proving it, and does not identify scalar potentials without a normalization. Here $Jw(t)=\int_0^tw(s)\,ds$.
notes.TorusEuler.PaperMeanParent: On $[0,T]\times\mathbb T^3$, supply smooth matrix fields $F,M$, an inverse $G$ with $GF=FG=I$, and a continuous time derivative $M_t$. Require $F_t=MF$, $\|G\|\le D$, $\|M\|\le L$, and $\langle-(M_t+M^2)w,w\rangle\le|w|^2$ for every $w$. In §4 these are $F=D_aX$, $G=F^{-1}$ and $M=(\nabla u)\circ X$. The formal data themselves need not arise from any velocity or volume-preserving flow. They isolate the identities needed by the endpoint inverse; positivity of $T$ and bounds such as $D\ge1$ are imposed by theorems using them.
notes.TorusEuler.PaperMeanParent.exists_integr: Let $T>0$ and suppose smooth periodic $F,M$ satisfy $F_t=MF$, with inverse $G$, bounds $\|G\|\le D$, $\|M\|\le L$, and $-(M_t+M^2)\le I$. For a smooth periodic label force $f_{\mathrm{lab}}(t,a)$, there is a smooth curve $L:[0,T]\to C^{0,1/2}(\mathbb T^3)$ whose values are $L(t,a)=-\int_0^tF(s,a)^Tf_{\mathrm{lab}}(s,a)\,ds$. In Theorem 4.2 one first sets $f_{\mathrm{lab}}=f\circ X$. This construction does not itself perform that composition or solve the endpoint problem.
notes.TorusEuler.PaperPhysicalStepBudget.hiera: Let $\mathsf D,\lambda\ge1$ and suppose the common step coefficient has been chosen to dominate all the specified costs, including $\Gamma_P\ge1$ and an exponent $b\ge6r$. If $\Gamma_P\mathsf D^b\lambda^{-1/12}\le1$, then $(\mathsf D^r)^6\lambda^{-1/12}\le1$. This is the precise implication supplied by the formal statement behind the sentence after (5.43). The hierarchy uses loss $\mathsf D^r$ and hence its sixth power here. The assertion is a numerical consequence of the coefficient choice; it does not independently prove any hierarchy estimate or select the frequency.
notes.TorusEuler.PaperSmoothMeanSolution: Fix smooth periodic coefficient fields $F,G,M$ with $G=F^{-1}$, $F_t=MF$ and the upper-curvature bound for the endpoint problem. A smooth mean solution consists of periodic fields $v,z,B,\mathsf q$ on $[0,T]$ satisfying $z_t=v$, $z(0)=z(T)=0$, $\operatorname{div}_a v=0$, $B=Fv$ and $B_t+MB+G^T\nabla_a\mathsf q=f\circ X$. All smoothness is joint in time and label, including derivatives within the closed interval. The physical trajectory displacement is $\xi=Fz$, and the Eulerian correction is $b=B\circ X^{-1}$. Thus $z$ and $B$ are not themselves Eulerian displacement and velocity. This definition does not impose a mean-zero normalization on the scalar pressure.
notes.TorusEuler.PaperSmoothMeanSolution.euler:
Let $u$ be a smooth periodic divergence-free parent on $[0,T]$, $T>0$, with flow $X$. Suppose a smooth periodic label solution has $z_t=v$, $z(0)=z(T)=0$, $\operatorname{div}_av=0$, $B=Fv$, and $B_t+MB+F^{-T}
abla_a\mathsf q=f_{\mathrm{lab}}$, with $F=D_aX$, $M=(
abla u)\circ X$. Its coefficient data also carry the inverse, gradient and $H^\#\le I$ bounds. Then $b=B\circ X^{-1}$ and $q=\mathsf q\circ X^{-1}$ are smooth periodic fields, $\operatorname{div}b=0$, and $b_t+u\cdot
abla b+b\cdot
abla u+
abla q=f_{\mathrm{lab}}\circ X^{-1}$. Recovering the paper's $f$ requires $f_{\mathrm{lab}}=f\circ X$.
notes.TorusEuler.PaperSmoothMeanSolution.exist: Let $T>0$. Suppose smooth periodic matrix fields $F,M$ satisfy $F_t=MF$, have a bounded inverse, and satisfy the gradient and upper displacement-Hessian bounds used by the mean inverse. Let a smooth periodic label solution satisfy $z_t=v$, $z(0)=z(T)=0$, $\operatorname{div}_av=0$ and $B_t+MB+F^{-T}\nabla_a\mathsf q=f_{\mathrm{lab}}$, with $B=Fv$. For a smooth half-Hölder source equal to $-J(F^Tf_{\mathrm{lab}})$, this solution satisfies $\mathbb P(Kv-J(\Omega v)+L)=c$ for some time-independent solenoidal $c$, with exactly the same label velocity. The coefficient representatives must equal $F^TF$ and $F^T(M^T-M)F$. This is a compatibility result for an existing solution. Here $Jw(t)=\int_0^tw(s)\,ds$.
notes.TorusEuler.PaperSmoothMeanSolution.mean_: Let $0<T\le1$ and suppose the smooth periodic parent coefficients satisfy $F_t=MF$, $G=F^{-1}$, $\|G\|\le D$ with $D\ge1$, $\|M\|\le L$ with $L\ge0$, and $-(M_t+M^2)\le I$ as quadratic forms. For the same smooth periodic forcing, take two smooth mean solutions with label displacements zero at both $0$ and $T$. The formal statement proves equality of their pulled-back physical means $B=Fz_t$ for every time in $[0,T]$. Hence their initial corrections agree. It compares existing solutions on the same interval; it does not establish existence or identify scalar pressures, whose additive time-dependent constants remain free.
notes.TorusEuler.PaperSmoothMeanSolution.stron: Suppose smooth periodic $F,M$ obey $F_t=MF$, $G=F^{-1}$, the inverse and gradient bounds, and $-(M_t+M^2)\le I$ on $[0,T]$, $T>0$. Let a smooth periodic mean solution have $B=Fv$, zero endpoint displacement, divergence-free $v$, and $B_t+MB+G^T\nabla_a\mathsf q=f_{\mathrm{lab}}$. Then $Kv_t+\nabla_a\mathsf q=F^Tf_{\mathrm{lab}}-2F^TMFv$, with $K=F^TF$. Taking $f_{\mathrm{lab}}=f\circ X$ gives (4.11), since $2F^TMF=2F^TF_t$. The equation holds at each time, using derivatives from within the closed interval at its endpoints.
notes.TorusEuler.PaperTerminalOffOrigin: For a field $u$ and terminal time $T$, this condition requires a local $C^m$ limit for each of $u(t)$ and its time derivative, for every integer $m\ge0$ and compact $K\subset\mathbb R^3\setminus\mathbb Z^3$. A local limit means a $C^m$ field on an open neighbourhood of $K$ and uniform convergence on $K$ of every spatial derivative through order $m$ as $t\uparrow T$ within $[0,T)$. The lattice is the set of representatives of the torus origin. The time derivative is defined relative to the half-open lifespan. Positivity of $T$ and the Euler equations are imposed elsewhere. This condition states the two limits of Proposition 8.4 without supplying existence or a smooth continuation.
notes.TorusEuler.PaperTerminalTime: For prescribed $T,u,p$, this condition requires a smooth periodic Euler solution on $[0,T)$, with $0<T<\infty$ and mean-zero pressure, admitting no longer smooth Euler solution whose velocity agrees there. It also requires $\int_0^T\|\operatorname{curl}u(t)\|_\infty\,dt=\infty$ and $\int_0^T\|\nabla u(t)\|_\infty\,dt=\infty$. These are nonnegative Lebesgue integrals; spatial norms are essential suprema over the unit cell, and the gradient uses its operator norm. The condition does not itself identify $T$ with a limit of activation times or prove its existence. Those identifications are made when all Section 8 conclusions are established for one construction.
notes.TorusEuler.PaperTerminalVelocityCurl: For a given field $u$ and real time $T$, this condition records a single finite bound for the essential supremum of $|u(t,x)|$ over $x\in[-1/2,1/2]^3$, valid for every $0\le t<T$. It also records $|\operatorname{curl}u(t,0)|\to\infty$ as $t\uparrow T$ within that interval: every prescribed threshold is exceeded at all sufficiently late times. In the periodic Euler application the cell represents $\mathbb T^3$ and $T=T_\infty>0$. The condition alone supplies neither positivity of $T$, periodicity, nor the Euler equations. Unlike the enlarged formal Proposition 8.2 conclusions, it contains no quantitative lower bound indexed by activation intervals.
notes.TorusEuler.PaperTheorem71Conclusions: For a given scheduled construction, this condition records smooth odd divergence-free periodic velocities $U_j$ on $[0,S_j]$, starting from the stationary sine shear. Residuals are bounded by $\lambda_{j+1}^{-3}$, Fourier support by $2\lambda_j^5$, and pressure Hessians above by $\sum_{i<j}\lambda_i^{-1}$ times the identity. It records the central gradient as the preceding gradient plus a switched rank-one wave and an error bounded by $\lambda_j^{-1/4}$. Crossing times have the prescribed coupling ratios and shear bounds and tend to a finite positive $T<S_j$. Oscillations are supported within distance $\lambda_{j-1}^{-1}$ of lattice points and bounded by $\lambda_j^{-1}$; the remaining increments are small in spatial $C^{m,1/2}$ for $m\le q_j$. This specifies conclusions for a construction; it does not assert existence.
notes.TorusEuler.PaperWaveCutoff: The formal object is a real function $\widetilde\chi$ that is smooth on $[0,T]$, takes values in $[0,1]$ there, and vanishes at times $t<t_0$ within that interval. It encodes the cutoff in (3.7). The function is defined at all real times, but no restriction is imposed outside $[0,T]$, and no condition says that it eventually reaches one. For $0<t_0<T$, smoothness and vanishing to the left give flatness at activation. The first wave is treated separately by choosing $t_0=0$ and the constant function one.
notes.TorusEuler.PaperWaveCutoff.derivativeSiz: For a smooth cutoff $\widetilde\chi$ on $[0,T]$, define the real supremum $\sup_{t\in[t_0,T]}|\widetilde\chi\,{}^{\prime}(t)|\gamma(t)$. The derivative is taken within $[0,T]$, including its one-sided values at the endpoints. If $0\le t_0\le T$, $T>0$, and $\gamma$ is continuous and nonnegative, compactness makes this a finite nonnegative number, equal to the quantity $\|\widetilde\chi\,{}^{\prime}\gamma\|_\infty$ in (5.48). The definition alone does not assume those properties of $\gamma$; with signed weights it is a supremum of the displayed product, not its absolute value. The formal real supremum has a default value when the set is empty or unbounded, so boundedness is established before using it as a norm.
notes.TorusEuler.PaperWaveCutoff.first: For the first wave the formal construction chooses activation time zero and $\widetilde\chi(t)=1$ for every real $t$. This satisfies the cutoff conditions on $[0,T]$: smoothness, range in $[0,1]$ and vanishing before activation within that interval, because there are no such times in $[0,T]$. Therefore the leading wave and its curl correction are not attenuated. The cutoff derivative vanishes, so this choice contributes no activation residual in (3.8). The formula specifies the first-wave cutoff; it does not assert the same choice for later activation times.
notes.TorusEuler.ParentLabelJetBound: For a real normed-space-valued field $f$ on $[0,T]\times\mathbb R^3$, this condition requires $\|D_a^j f(t,a)\|\le C_j\mathsf D^{pj+c}$ at every nonnegative integer order $j$ and every point. The same natural-number slope $p$ and offset $c$ apply at every order. Derivatives are multilinear maps with operator norm, including order zero. The definition asserts these inequalities but imposes no smoothness condition independently; the coefficient theorems provide smoothness and the bounds together. Proposition 5.1 uses such polynomial bounds before inserting the radius weights, and coordinate derivative sums are recovered up to order-dependent constants.
notes.TorusEuler.ParentLabelJetBound.weighted_: All $C_j$ are nonnegative, $\mathsf D\ge1$ and $\ell_*\ge0$; the norms use multilinear derivatives, not a separately normalized coordinate sum. If $\lVert D_a^j f\rVert\le C_j\mathsf D^{pj+c}$ and $\ell_*\mathsf D^p\le1$, the weighted derivative sum is at most $(\sum_{j\le n}C_j)\mathsf D^c$. Thus the remaining exponent is independent of $n$. This is the final summation step behind (5.8); the polynomial derivative bound is an input to it.
notes.TorusEuler.RealTorusFourierBand: For a continuous real vector field on $\mathbb T^3=\mathbb R^3/\mathbb Z^3$, frequency support at most $\Lambda$ means that its complex Fourier coefficient at every $\xi\in\mathbb Z^3$ with Euclidean length $|\xi|>\Lambda$ is zero. The Fourier convention is $e^{2\pi i\xi\cdot x}$. Frequencies on the boundary are permitted, and the condition does not remove the zero mode. This is the definition introduced in §5.1. The parent hypotheses use radii $2\mathsf D$ and $4\mathsf D$ for velocity and residual; the next truncated stage uses $2\Lambda$ and $4\Lambda$. The condition alone says nothing about time regularity or incompressibility.
notes.TorusEuler.ReferenceAmplitude.integrated: Let $0\le\varepsilon\le1$, $T\ge2$, $0\le t\le T$, and $\eta\ge0$. Suppose $Y$ is continuous on $[0,T]$ and $|Y|\le1$ there. With $\cos\varphi(\tau)=(1+\varepsilon^2\tau^4/4)^{-1/2}$, the formal statement proves $0\le\int_0^t(1+|Y|)^2\eta/\cos\varphi\le4T^3\eta$. The number $\eta$ here is a constant bound for an amplitude error operator, not the frozen coupling $B_{32}(t_0)$. No Riccati equation is assumed. This is the integral estimate that converts a polynomial coefficient error into a polynomial comparison error after dividing by the reference amplitude.
notes.TorusEuler.ReferenceAmplitude.log_growin: At a fixed time let $k\cdot\mathbf a=0$ in an orthonormal frame, with $\lambda\ne0$, $S>0$, $T\ge1$, $|\zeta_1|\le T^2$, $|\zeta_2|\le T$, and $\zeta_3\ge1/2$. Assume $|Y|\le1$ and $\max\{|h-1|,|l|\}\le d\le1/2$, where $h=\alpha_2/a_{\rm ref}$, $l=-(\alpha_1+Y\alpha_2)/(a_{\rm ref}\cos\varphi)$ and $a_{\rm ref}=\exp\int_0^\tau Y$. Then $|\log(|\mathbf a|/a_{\rm ref})|\le2d+20T^4S^{-2}$. The closeness hypothesis makes $\alpha_2$ and $|\mathbf a|$ positive, so the logarithm has its usual meaning. The conclusion is a pointwise error bound, not yet (2.18); further smallness makes the right side at most $\varepsilon$.
notes.TorusEuler.ReferenceAmplitude.orthonorma: In a real inner-product space with a three-vector orthonormal basis, suppose the coordinates of $\mathbf a$ are $(-U/S,V,(XU-QV)/(SZ))$, with $V>0$, $Z\ne0$ and $S>0$. Then $|\mathbf a|=V\sqrt{1+S^{-2}[(U/V)^2+((X(U/V)-Q)/Z)^2]}$. Taking $(X,Q,Z)=\zeta$, $U=-\alpha_1$, and $V=\alpha_2$ gives the paper’s identity $|\mathbf a|^2=\alpha_2^2+S^{-2}(\alpha_1^2+\alpha_3^2)$ after using transversality. The coordinate relations are hypotheses here. This result is purely geometric and does not require an amplitude differential equation.
notes.TorusEuler.ReferenceAmplitude.raw_ratio_: For arbitrary real functions $Y,U,V$, put $a_{\rm ref}(t)=\exp\int_0^tY$, $s(t)=(1+\varepsilon^2t^4/4)^{-1/2}$, $h=V/a_{\rm ref}$ and $l=(U-YV)/(s a_{\rm ref})$. If $\max\{|h(t)-1|,|l(t)|\}\le d\le1/2$, then $V(t)>0$ and $|U(t)/V(t)-Y(t)|\le2d$. Both $s$ and $a_{\rm ref}$ are positive by their definitions. For the paper’s amplitude, $U=-\alpha_1$ and $V=\alpha_2$, so the error is $|\alpha_1/\alpha_2+Y|$. No differential equation is assumed; the result extracts the ratio bound from the normalized comparison.

Let $a_{\rm ref}(t)=\exp\int_0^tY$ and $s(t)=(1+\varepsilon^2t^4/4)^{-1/2}$. Define $h=V/a_{\rm ref}$ and $l=(U-YV)/(s a_{\rm ref})$. At any time with $V(t)\ne0$, the formal statement gives $U/V=Y+s\,l/h$. For $(U,V)=(-\alpha_1,\alpha_2)$ this is the paper’s identity $\alpha_1/\alpha_2+Y=-l\cos\varphi/h$. The nonzero assumption makes $h\ne0$; the positive denominators $s$ and $a_{\rm ref}$ require no additional assumptions. The identity itself gives neither positivity nor a small-error estimate.
notes.TorusEuler.ReferenceAmplitude.reference_: Let $A(t)>0$ and $a_{\rm ref}(t)=\exp\int_0^tY$. If $|\log(A(t)/a_{\rm ref}(t))|\le\varepsilon$, then $\exp(-\varepsilon)a_{\rm ref}(t)\le A(t)\le\exp(\varepsilon)a_{\rm ref}(t)$. The formal statement applies at one time to arbitrary functions $A,Y$; no wave equation or regularity of $Y$ is required for this implication. In Proposition 2.8, $A=|\mathbf a|$ and Lemma 2.6 supplies the positive amplitude and logarithmic bound on the whole interval. Positivity is essential for this ordinary interpretation of the logarithm.
notes.TorusEuler.ReferenceComparison.hasDerivW: On $[0,T]$, suppose $Y$ satisfies the reference Riccati equation. At $t\in[0,T]$, assume $(U,V)$ satisfies the reference linear equations with added operator $R(t)$. Set $s=\cos\varphi$, $a_{\rm ref}=\exp\int_0^tY$, $h=V/a_{\rm ref}$ and $l=(U-YV)/(sa_{\rm ref})$. Then $(h,l)$ has derivative $(sl,-2s(1+e)l)+QRQ^{-1}(h,l)$, where $e=(Y+\varepsilon t\sin(2\varphi)/4)/s-1$ and $Q(U,V)=(V,(U-YV)/s)$. Derivatives are taken within the time interval, including its endpoints. The statement is an exact coordinate identity with no error bound. The paper’s matrix acts on $(-U,V)=(\alpha_1,\alpha_2)$, which accounts for its different signs.
notes.TorusEuler.ReferenceComparison.norm_movi: At one time let the frame be orthonormal, $k\cdot\mathbf b=0$, $\lambda\ne0$, $S\ge1$, $|\zeta_1|,|\zeta_2|\le S$, $1/2\le\zeta_3\le3/2$, $|Y|\le1$, and $|\zeta_1-\varepsilon t^2/2|\le1/2$. For $h=\beta_2/a_{\rm ref}$ and $l=-(\beta_1+Y\beta_2)/(a_{\rm ref}\cos\varphi)$, the formal statement gives $|\mathbf b|\le9a_{\rm ref}\max\{|h|,|l|\}$ and $\max\{|h|,|l|\}\le7S|\mathbf b|/a_{\rm ref}$. The vector norm is Euclidean and the pair norm is the maximum norm. These pointwise inequalities quantify the factor $S$ in recovering normalized coordinates; no amplitude differential equation is assumed.
notes.TorusEuler.ReferenceComparison.norm_norm: At any real time $t$, set $s=(1+\varepsilon^2t^4/4)^{-1/2}$ and $Q(U,V)=(V,(U-Y(t)V)/s)$. For any linear operator $R(t)$ on real pairs, the formal statement gives $\|QRQ^{-1}\|\le(1+|Y(t)|)^2\|R(t)\|/s$. The pair norm and its induced operator norm are maximum norms. This becomes the paper’s polynomial bound after using $|Y|\le1$, $1/s\le T^2$, and a polynomial estimate for $R$. The displayed formal result is an exact pointwise inequality for arbitrary $Y$ and $R$, so it does not itself supply those three estimates.
notes.TorusEuler.ReferenceComparison.normalize: For real functions $Y,U,V$, let $a_{\rm ref}(t)=\exp\int_0^tY$ and $s(t)=(1+\varepsilon^2t^4/4)^{-1/2}$. The formal object is $(V/a_{\rm ref},(U-YV)/(s a_{\rm ref}))$. With $U=-\alpha_1$, $V=\alpha_2$ and $s=\cos\varphi$, it is exactly $(h,l)$ from (2.15). Both denominators are strictly positive. Real pairs carry the maximum norm, so a bound on the norm of this pair is a bound on both components. The definition does not assume a reference or perturbed differential equation; such equations enter the comparison theorems.
notes.TorusEuler.ReferenceComparison.unscaledC: At time $t$, put $s=(1+\varepsilon^2t^4/4)^{-1/2}$. The formal object is the linear map $Q(U,V)=(V,(U-Y(t)V)/s)$. Dividing this pair by $a_{\rm ref}(t)$ gives the normalized coordinates $(h,l)$. The paper instead writes its matrix on $(\alpha_1,\alpha_2)=(-U,V)$, hence its lower left entry is $-1/s$ rather than $1/s$. The maps agree after that sign change. Since $s>0$ for every real $\varepsilon,t$, the map is invertible wherever $Y(t)$ is defined. No differential equation is part of this definition.

At time $t$, put $s=(1+\varepsilon^2t^4/4)^{-1/2}$. The formal object maps $(h,l)$ to $(Y(t)h+sl,h)$. It is the inverse of $Q(U,V)=(V,(U-Y(t)V)/s)$; multiplying by $a_{\rm ref}$ then recovers $(U,V)$. Because $U=-\alpha_1$, the inverse matrix printed in the paper has first row $(-Y,-s)$ instead. This sign convention explains the apparent discrepancy. The positive value of $s$ makes the inverse meaningful for all real inputs, independently of whether $Y$ solves the Riccati equation.
notes.TorusEuler.ReferencePropagator.hasDerivW: Let $Y$ solve the Riccati equation on $[0,T]$. At $t\in[0,T]$, suppose $(U,V)$ satisfies $U'=-\varepsilon t\sin(2\varphi)U+\cos^2\varphi(1-\varepsilon\tan\varphi)V$ and $V'=U$. Put $a_{\rm ref}=\exp\int_0^tY$, $h=V/a_{\rm ref}$, $l=(U-YV)/(a_{\rm ref}\cos\varphi)$ and $e=(Y+\varepsilon t\sin(2\varphi)/4)/\cos\varphi-1$. The formal statement gives $h\prime=l\cos\varphi$ and $l'=-2(1+e)l\cos\varphi$. Derivatives are taken within $[0,T]$. This is (2.16) with $(U,V)=(-\alpha_1,\alpha_2)$; positivity or smallness of $e$ is not required for the identity itself.
notes.TorusEuler.ReferencePropagator.normalize: Let $\varepsilon>0$, let $Y$ solve the reference Riccati equation on $[0,T]$ with $Y(0)=1$, and let $(U,V)$ solve the unperturbed reference linear system there. Define $h=V/a_{\rm ref}$ and $l=(U-YV)/(a_{\rm ref}\cos\varphi)$. For $0\le a\le b\le T$, the formal statement gives $\sqrt{h(b)^2+l(b)^2}\le2\sqrt{h(a)^2+l(a)^2}$. This is explicitly the Euclidean norm, unlike the maximum norm used for many pair estimates elsewhere. The factor $2$ is uniform in $\varepsilon,a,b,T$, and this theorem does not impose $\varepsilon\le1$. It proves an estimate for every solution, hence the corresponding forward propagator bound.
notes.TorusEuler.ReferencePropagator.triangula: Let $a\le b$, and let $s,e$ be continuous and nonnegative on $[a,b]$. Set $d(a,t)=\exp(-\int_a^t2s(1+e))$ and $q(a,b)=\int_a^b s(t)d(a,t)\,dt$. The formal statement gives $0<d(a,b)\le1$ and $0\le q(a,b)\le(1-d(a,b))/2$. Thus the transfer from $l$ into $h$ is bounded by half the decrease of its absolute amplitude. The result applies to arbitrary continuous nonnegative coefficients, including $s=\cos\varphi$ and the reference deviation. It estimates coefficients of the explicit solution formula and does not itself quantify over solutions.

Let $a\le b$, with continuous nonnegative functions $s,e$ on $[a,b]$. Suppose $h\prime=sl$ and $l'=-2s(1+e)l$ throughout that interval, using one-sided derivatives at the endpoints. Then $|h(b)|+|l(b)|\le|h(a)|+|l(a)|$. This is the contraction used in Section 2.2.2 with $s=\cos\varphi$ and the bounded deviation of the reference solution. The formal statement is more general than that specialization: neither a Riccati equation nor bounds on $\varepsilon$ appear, because nonnegativity of the two coefficient functions is the only property needed here.

Let $s,e$ be continuous on $[a,b]$, and let $h,l$ satisfy $h\prime=sl$, $l'=-2s(1+e)l$ there. For $t\in[a,b]$, set $d(a,t)=\exp(-\int_a^t2s(1+e))$ and $q(a,t)=\int_a^t s(u)d(a,u)\,du$. The formal statement gives $l(t)=d(a,t)l(a)$ and $h(t)=h(a)+q(a,t)l(a)$. The result uses derivatives within the closed interval and permits coefficients of either sign. Decay and contraction require the separate nonnegativity hypotheses used later. With $s=\cos\varphi$, this is the solution formula behind (2.16).
notes.TorusEuler.ReferenceRiccati.actual_coupl:
Let $0<\varepsilon\le1/16$, $T\ge2$, $\varphi=\arctan(\varepsilon	au^2/2)$, and $Y=(1+e)\cos\varphi-\varepsilon	au\sin(2\varphi)/4$, with $0\le e\le\varepsilon/8$ on $[0,\infty)$. Suppose scalar functions $n,h$ differ from the reference expressions for $
u_+/
u,\eta_+/
u$ by at most $\varepsilon/(8T^2)$ on $[0,T]$. Then $n\ge\varepsilon/2$ throughout $[0,T]$. On $[\sqrt2/\varepsilon,T]$, $|n-1|\le\varepsilon$ and $|(h/n)/\cos\varphi-1|\le1/2$. The result assumes the additive comparison and the bounded-deviation representation; it does not assert that $n,h$ arise from a wave. No differential equation for $Y$ is needed in this algebraic comparison.
notes.TorusEuler.ReferenceRiccati.amplitude_in: Let $Y$ be continuous on $[0,\infty)$, with $Y\le1$, and suppose $\int_0^{\tau_m}Y\ge\varepsilon^{-1/2}-1$. Assume $2\varepsilon\le1$, $\tau_m\in[0,T]$, and $\exp(-\varepsilon)a_{\rm ref}\le A\le\exp(\varepsilon)a_{\rm ref}$ on $[0,T]$, where $a_{\rm ref}=\exp\int_0^\tau Y$. For $\tau\in[0,1]$ with $\tau\le T$, the formal statement proves $A(\tau)\le\exp(3-\varepsilon^{-1/2})A(\tau_m)$. This is slightly sharper than replacing $A(\tau_m)$ by the maximum over $[0,T]$. The formal expression $\varepsilon^{-1/2}$ means $1/\sqrt\varepsilon$; the application has $\varepsilon>0$.
notes.TorusEuler.ReferenceRiccati.amplitude_la: Let $0<\varepsilon\le1$, $\tau_m\in[2/\varepsilon,3/\varepsilon]$, and $\tau_m\le\tau\le T$. Suppose continuous $Y$ has the bounded-deviation representation (2.13), $0\le e\le\varepsilon/8$, and $a_{\rm ref}=\exp\int_0^\tau Y$ attains its maximum on $[0,T]$ at $\tau_m$. Assume $ca_{\rm ref}\le A\le Ca_{\rm ref}$ there, with $c,C>0$, and $M=\max_{[0,T]}A$. If $0\le k_{\min},k_{\max}$ and $k_{\min}x\le k\le k_{\max}x$, $x=\varepsilon\tau^2/2$, then $k_{\min}(c/C)\sqrt{x/\varepsilon}\le kA(\tau)/M\le3\exp(2)k_{\max}(C/c)\sqrt{x/\varepsilon}$. Here $k$ represents the wave-number ratio $|k(\tau)|/\lambda$. This version derives the needed reference amplitude-ratio identity from the representation of $Y$.
notes.TorusEuler.ReferenceRiccati.amplitude_ra: Let $c,C>0$, $\tau_m,\tau\in[0,T]$, and $a_{\rm ref}(t)=\exp\int_0^tY$. Suppose $a_{\rm ref}(t)\le a_{\rm ref}(\tau_m)$ on $[0,T]$ and $ca_{\rm ref}(t)\le A(t)\le Ca_{\rm ref}(t)$ there. If $M$ is an attained maximum of $A$ on that interval, then $(c/C)a_{\rm ref}(\tau)/a_{\rm ref}(\tau_m)\le A(\tau)/M\le(C/c)a_{\rm ref}(\tau)/a_{\rm ref}(\tau_m)$. The positivity assumptions ensure nonzero denominators. The formal result assumes existence of $M$ and the reference maximum; it does not prove either. In the crossing argument, $A=|\mathbf a|$ and $c,C=\exp(\mp\varepsilon)$.
notes.TorusEuler.ReferenceRiccati.couplingRati: Let $x=\varepsilon\tau^2/2\ge1$, $s=(1+x^2)^{-1/2}$, and suppose a real number $\rho$ satisfies $|\rho/s-1|\le1/2$. Then $1/(4x)\le\rho\le3/(2x)$. In Proposition 2.8, $s=\cos\varphi$ and $\rho=\eta_+/\nu_+$. The hypothesis $x\ge1$ makes all reciprocals positive. The formal statement is an algebraic consequence of the relative comparison; it does not require continuity or prove a crossing, which use this estimate on an interval.
notes.TorusEuler.ReferenceRiccati.coupling_err: Assume $T\ge2$, $\delta\ge0$, and nonnegative integers $p,C_0$ with $p+2\le C_0$. Let a real coefficient $C$ satisfy $8C\le C_0$. If $C_0T^{C_0}\delta\le\varepsilon$, then $CT^p\delta\le\varepsilon/(8T^2)$. This is the precise arithmetic step used to obtain the coupling error margin in Section 2.2.4 from (2.7). The exponents are natural numbers; the formal statement does not quantify over arbitrary real exponents. It imposes no positivity on $C$, although the application uses a nonnegative error constant.
notes.TorusEuler.ReferenceRiccati.deviation_ex: For $0<\varepsilon\le1$ and $\varphi(\tau)=\arctan(\varepsilon\tau^2/2)$, the formal statement constructs a real function $e$ with $e(0)=0$, $e'=\cos\varphi[-2e-e^2+(\varepsilon/2)\sin\varphi\cos\varphi]$ on $[0,\infty)$, and $0\le e\le\varepsilon/8$ there. Derivatives at zero are taken from the right. The function is defined at negative times too, but the equation and bound impose no conditions there. This is existence with an invariant interval for the deviation; uniqueness and the corresponding Riccati solution $Y$ are not conclusions of this declaration.
notes.TorusEuler.ReferenceRiccati.deviation_ze: For real $\varepsilon$ and a function $Y$ with $Y(0)=1$, define $e(\tau)=[Y(\tau)+\varepsilon\tau\sin(2\varphi)/4]/\cos\varphi-1$, with $\varphi=\arctan(\varepsilon\tau^2/2)$. The formal statement proves $e(0)=0$, since $\varphi(0)=0$. It uses only the initial value of $Y$, not its differential equation or continuity. This supplies the initial condition in the deviation equation derived in the proof of Lemma 2.5; the evolution and interval bound for $e$ are separate conclusions.
notes.TorusEuler.ReferenceRiccati.hasDerivAt_s: For arbitrary real $\varepsilon,\tau$, let $s(\tau)=(1+\varepsilon^2\tau^4/4)^{-1/2}=\cos\varphi(\tau)$, where $\varphi=\arctan(\varepsilon\tau^2/2)$. The formal statement gives $s'=-(\varepsilon\tau\sin(2\varphi)/2)s$. Since $s>0$, division by $s$ yields $(\log\cos\varphi)\prime=-\varepsilon\tau\sin(2\varphi)/2$. The displayed formal conclusion is the derivative of $s$ itself; it does not separately state the derivative of $\varphi$ or of its logarithm. No Riccati solution or positive-parameter hypothesis is needed.
notes.TorusEuler.ReferenceRiccati.hasDerivWith: Let $\varphi(\tau)=\arctan(\varepsilon\tau^2/2)$ and suppose $Y'=\cos^2\varphi(1-\varepsilon\tan\varphi)-\varepsilon\tau\sin(2\varphi)Y-Y^2$ at a given time. Define $e=[Y+\varepsilon\tau\sin(2\varphi)/4]/\cos\varphi-1$. The formal statement gives $e'=\cos\varphi[-2e-e^2+(\varepsilon/2)\sin\varphi\cos\varphi]$ at that time. The derivative may be restricted to an arbitrary time set, so the same calculation covers one-sided endpoint derivatives. The initial condition $e(0)=0$ requires $Y(0)=1$ separately, and no invariant-interval bound is asserted here.

Let $Y$ be continuous on $[0,\infty)$ and set $a_{\rm ref}(\tau)=\exp\int_0^\tau Y$. For every $\tau\ge0$, the formal statement proves $a_{\rm ref}\prime(\tau)=Y(\tau)a_{\rm ref}(\tau)$, with a right derivative at zero. Its named first reference component is $U=Ya_{\rm ref}$; the paper’s first amplitude component is $\alpha_1=-U$, so this derivative also says $\alpha_2\prime=-\alpha_1$. The result requires continuity but not the Riccati equation. Positivity of the exponential makes $Y=a_{\rm ref}\prime/a_{\rm ref}$ legitimate.
notes.TorusEuler.ReferenceRiccati.inv_sq_windo: Assume $0\le\varepsilon\le1$, $T\ge2$ and $0\le\tau\le T$. Then $(1+\varepsilon^2\tau^4/4)^{-1/2}\ge T^{-2}$. Since this quantity equals $\cos\varphi$ for $\varphi=\arctan(\varepsilon\tau^2/2)$, the inequality is equivalent to $1/\cos\varphi\le T^2$. This is the polynomial denominator bound used when conjugating the amplitude error in Section 2.2.3. The formal statement uses only the parameter and time bounds; it is independent of the wave, the Riccati solution and the coefficient error.
notes.TorusEuler.ReferenceRiccati.inv_two_mul_: Put $x=\varepsilon\tau^2/2$ and assume $x\ge1$. The formal statement proves $(2x)^{-1}\le(1+x^2)^{-1/2}$. With $x=\tan\varphi$ and $\varphi=\arctan x$, this is $1/(2\tan\varphi)\le\cos\varphi$, the lower comparison used after the reference peak. Only $x\ge1$ is required; no independent positivity assumption on $\varepsilon$ or time bound is stated. The hypothesis makes all denominators nonzero and positive.
notes.TorusEuler.ReferenceRiccati.referenceEta: For real $\varepsilon,\tau$ and a function $Y$, put $x=\varepsilon\tau^2/2$ and $s=(1+x^2)^{-1/2}$. The formal object is $h_0=[-1+\varepsilon x+2(1+x^2)Y(\tau)^2+2\varepsilon\tau xY(\tau)]s$. With $x=\tan\varphi$, this is the unreduced reference value of $\eta_+/\nu$ in Section 2.2.4. It is not the ratio $\eta_+/\nu_+$; that requires division by the first reference coupling. The definition assumes no Riccati equation or smallness, so the cancellation and late-time estimates require the representation and bound for $Y$.
notes.TorusEuler.ReferenceRiccati.referenceNu:
For real $\varepsilon,	au$ and a function $Y$, set $x=\varepsilon	au^2/2$, $s=(1+x^2)^{-1/2}$. The formal object is $n_0=(x+\varepsilon+2\varepsilon	au Y(	au))s$. In the reference wave this equals $\sin\varphi+\varepsilon\cos\varphi+2\varepsilon	au Y\cos\varphi$, the normalized value $
u_+/
u$ used in Section 2.2.4. Thus it is dimensionless, not the physical coupling $
u_+$ itself. At $	au=0$ it equals $\varepsilon$ for every $Y$. Positivity at later times and the late bound near one are additional results.
notes.TorusEuler.ReferenceRiccati.referenceNu_: Let $0<\varepsilon\le1$, $0\le\tau\le\sqrt2/\varepsilon$, and $\varphi=\arctan(\varepsilon\tau^2/2)$. Suppose $Y=(1+e)\cos\varphi-\varepsilon\tau\sin(2\varphi)/4$ and $e(\tau)\ge0$. Then the reference expression $\sin\varphi+\varepsilon\cos\varphi+2\varepsilon\tau Y\cos\varphi$ is at least $\varepsilon$. This is the lower bound for $\nu_+/\nu$ in the early range of Lemma 2.7. The formal statement does not need the upper bound $e\le\varepsilon/8$ or a differential equation for $Y$; it uses only the representation and nonnegativity at this time.
notes.TorusEuler.ReferenceRiccati.referenceU_z: Assume $Y(0)=1$ and define $a_{\rm ref}(\tau)=\exp\int_0^\tau Y$, $U=Ya_{\rm ref}$. The formal statement gives $U(0)=1$, because the integral over $[0,0]$ is zero. In the paper, $U=-\alpha_1$, so the corresponding initial value is $\alpha_1(0)=-1$. This one-coordinate equality is only part of the reference initial data $(-1,1)$; the second component is established separately. No regularity or Riccati equation for $Y$ is needed for this initial-value calculation.
notes.TorusEuler.ReferenceRiccati.referenceV: For a real function $Y$, the formal object is $a_{\rm ref}(\tau)=\exp(\int_0^\tau Y(t)\,dt)$. It is positive and equals one at zero. When $Y$ is continuous on the nonnegative half-line, its derivative is $Ya_{\rm ref}$ there, and a Riccati solution gives the reference amplitude of Lemma 2.5. The definition accepts all real times and all functions. The interval integral is oriented for negative upper limits and assigned zero for nonintegrable integrands; regularity assumptions in the reference theorem ensure the ordinary integral interpretation on $\tau\ge0$.
notes.TorusEuler.ReferenceRiccati.referenceV_l: Let $a\ge0$ and let $Y$ be continuous on $[0,\infty)$, with $Y\ge0$ on $[0,a]$ and $Y\le0$ on $[a,\infty)$. Then $a_{\rm ref}(t)=\exp\int_0^tY$ satisfies $a_{\rm ref}(t)\le a_{\rm ref}(a)$ for every $t\ge0$. The paper applies this with $a=\tau_m$, the unique zero of its reference slope. The formal statement requires only weak sign inequalities and does not assert uniqueness of the maximum or require a Riccati equation. The strict signs supplied by Lemma 2.5 are more than this step needs.
notes.TorusEuler.ReferenceRiccati.referenceV_r: Let $\varphi(t)=\arctan(\varepsilon t^2/2)$ and suppose $Y$ is continuous on $[0,\infty)$ with $Y=(1+e)\cos\varphi-\varepsilon t\sin(2\varphi)/4$. For $0\le a\le b$, put $a_{\rm ref}(t)=\exp\int_0^tY$. The formal statement proves $a_{\rm ref}(b)/a_{\rm ref}(a)=\sqrt{\cos\varphi(b)/\cos\varphi(a)}\exp\int_a^b(1+e)\cos\varphi$. This is the ratio formula used after the reference peak, but the theorem applies to any ordered nonnegative times. Neither the Riccati equation, positivity of $\varepsilon$, nor bounds on $e$ are required for this identity.
notes.TorusEuler.ReferenceRiccati.referenceV_z: For any real function $Y$, set $a_{\rm ref}(\tau)=\exp\int_0^\tau Y$. The formal statement gives $a_{\rm ref}(0)=1$. It needs no continuity, integrability or differential equation because the interval has zero length. This is the second component $\alpha_2(0)=1$ of the reference initial data in Section 2.2.2. It does not state the first initial component or assert that this function solves the amplitude equation; those require further identities and the relevant regularity assumptions.
notes.TorusEuler.ReferenceRiccati.referenceY: For arbitrary real $\varepsilon$ and a real function $e$, the formal object is $Y(\tau)=(1+e(\tau))s(\tau)-\varepsilon\tau x(\tau)s(\tau)^2/2$, where $x=\varepsilon\tau^2/2$ and $s=(1+x^2)^{-1/2}$. With $s=\cos\varphi$ and $xs=\sin\varphi$, this is (2.13): $Y=(1+e)\cos\varphi-\varepsilon\tau\sin(2\varphi)/4$. The definition places no bound or differential equation on $e$. Thus the formula alone supplies neither $0\le e\le\varepsilon/8$ nor a solution of (2.12); those are separate assertions in Lemma 2.5.
notes.TorusEuler.ReferenceRiccati.referenceY_n: Let $0<\varepsilon\le1$ and $\varepsilon\tau=3$. Suppose $e(\tau)\le\varepsilon/8$ and set $\varphi=\arctan(\varepsilon\tau^2/2)$, $Y=(1+e)\cos\varphi-\varepsilon\tau\sin(2\varphi)/4$. The formal statement proves $Y(\tau)<0$. No differential equation or lower bound on $e$ is needed for this pointwise sign calculation. This gives the upper sign in the proof that the reference amplitude peaks between $2/\varepsilon$ and $3/\varepsilon$; existence and uniqueness of that peak require the later Riccati argument.
notes.TorusEuler.ReferenceRiccati.referenceY_p: Assume $\varepsilon\ge0$, $\varepsilon\tau\le2$, and $e(\tau)\ge0$. For $\varphi=\arctan(\varepsilon\tau^2/2)$, the formal statement proves $(1+e(\tau))\cos\varphi-\varepsilon\tau\sin(2\varphi)/4>0$. Applied to the deviation of the reference Riccati solution for $\tau\ge0$, this is the positive sign before the reference peak in Lemma 2.5. The algebraic statement itself also permits negative $\tau$ and $\varepsilon=0$ and needs no differential equation or upper bound on $e$. Its extra domain does not extend the Riccati existence theorem to negative time.
notes.TorusEuler.ReferenceRiccati.reference_am: Let $Y$ satisfy the reference Riccati equation on $[0,\infty)$. Define $V(\tau)=\exp\int_0^\tau Y$ and $U(\tau)=Y(\tau)V(\tau)$. Then $V'=U$ and $U'=\cos^2\varphi(1-\varepsilon\tan\varphi)V-\varepsilon\tau\sin(2\varphi)U$ for every $\tau\ge0$, with right derivatives at zero. Since $(\alpha_1,\alpha_2)=(-U,V)$, these are exactly the reference amplitude equations (2.5). The formal statement does not require $Y(0)=1$; to obtain the particular initial data $(-1,1)$, that initial condition must also be imposed.
notes.TorusEuler.ReferenceRiccati.reference_co:
Let $0<\varepsilon\le1$, $	au\ge\sqrt2/\varepsilon$, and $\varphi=\arctan(\varepsilon	au^2/2)$. Suppose $Y=(1+e)\cos\varphi-\varepsilon	au\sin(2\varphi)/4$ and $0\le e(	au)\le\varepsilon/8$. For the reference expressions $n_0=
u_+/
u$ and $h_0=\eta_+/
u$, the formal statement proves $|n_0-1|\le7\varepsilon^2$ and $|h_0/\cos\varphi-1|\le2\varepsilon$. These are explicit versions of the two estimates following (2.22). The second expression is divided by the frozen $
u$, not by $
u_+$; comparison of $\eta_+/
u_+$ requires the separate bound for $n_0$ and the wave perturbation estimates.
notes.TorusEuler.ReferenceRiccati.reference_ta: Let $0<\varepsilon\le1$ and $2/\varepsilon\le a\le b$. Suppose $Y$ is continuous on $[0,\infty)$ with $Y=(1+e)\cos\varphi-\varepsilon t\sin(2\varphi)/4$, $0\le e\le\varepsilon/8$, and $\varphi=\arctan(\varepsilon t^2/2)$. Then $0\le\int_a^b(1+e)\cos\varphi\,dt\le2$. This is the uniform tail bound used in the amplitude-ratio formula after the reference peak. It holds for any starting time at least $2/\varepsilon$, without assuming that $a$ is a zero of $Y$ or that $Y$ solves the Riccati equation.
notes.TorusEuler.ReferenceRiccati.riccati_abs_: Let $0<\varepsilon\le1$ and suppose $Y(0)=1$ and $Y$ solves $Y'=\cos^2\varphi(1-\varepsilon\tan\varphi)-\varepsilon\tau\sin(2\varphi)Y-Y^2$ for all $\tau\ge0$, with $\varphi=\arctan(\varepsilon\tau^2/2)$. Then $|Y(\tau)|\le1$ throughout that half-line. The formal statement is a bound for any solution already defined there; it does not itself prove existence. It supplies both signs of the absolute bound in Lemma 2.5, whereas the paper’s particular proof sentence $Y\le1$ concerns only the upper bound.
notes.TorusEuler.ReferenceRiccati.riccati_gain: Let $0<\varepsilon\le1$ and $\tau_m\ge2/\varepsilon$. Suppose $Y$ is continuous on $[0,\infty)$, nonnegative on $[0,\tau_m]$, and has the form $Y=(1+e)\cos\varphi-\varepsilon\tau\sin(2\varphi)/4$, with $0\le e\le\varepsilon/8$ and $\varphi=\arctan(\varepsilon\tau^2/2)$. The formal statement gives $\int_0^{\tau_m}Y\ge1/\sqrt\varepsilon-1$. Since $a_{\rm ref}=\exp\int_0^\tau Y$, this is $\log a_{\rm ref}(\tau_m)\ge\varepsilon^{-1/2}-1$. The theorem assumes the sign and representation and does not require that $\tau_m$ be the unique zero. It records the final gain, rather than the intermediate inequalities in the paper’s proof.
notes.TorusEuler.ReferenceRiccati.riccati_turn: Let $0<\varepsilon\le1$. Suppose $Y$ solves the Riccati equation on $[0,\infty)$ and $Y=(1+e)\cos\varphi-\varepsilon\tau\sin(2\varphi)/4$, where $\varphi=\arctan(\varepsilon\tau^2/2)$ and $0\le e\le\varepsilon/8$. The formal statement gives $\tau_m\in[2/\varepsilon,3/\varepsilon]$ with $Y(\tau_m)=0$, $Y>0$ on $[0,\tau_m)$, and $Y<0$ on $(\tau_m,\infty)$. These strict signs imply that there is no other nonnegative zero. The statement presupposes a global solution and its representation; it does not construct them or assert an amplitude estimate.
notes.TorusEuler.ReferenceRiccati.s_le_inv_x: Put $x=\varepsilon\tau^2/2$ and assume $x>0$. Then $(1+x^2)^{-1/2}\le1/x$. With $\varphi=\arctan x$, this is $\cos\varphi\le1/\tan\varphi$, used with the corresponding lower bound when locating a crossing. The formal statement needs only positivity of $x$, which excludes division by zero. It neither assumes a wave equation nor claims that this estimate is sharp near $x=0$; the crossing argument uses it in the late range $x\ge1$.
notes.TorusEuler.ReferenceRiccati.x: The formal object is $x(\tau)=\varepsilon\tau^2/2$ for arbitrary real $\varepsilon,\tau$. It represents $\tan\varphi$ for the reference angle $\varphi=\arctan x$. For $\varepsilon\ge0$ and $\tau\ge0$, this is the limiting wave-vector turning law in (2.4). The definition does not use the actual perturbed wave vector, so it does not assert $x=(k\cdot E_1)/(k\cdot E_3)$ at finite shear. Estimates comparing the scaled wave coordinates with $(x,-\varepsilon\tau,1)$ establish the relation to the physical wave.
notes.TorusEuler.ReferenceRiccati.x_bounds_of_: If $\varepsilon>0$ and $2/\varepsilon\le\tau_m\le3/\varepsilon$, then $2/\varepsilon\le\varepsilon\tau_m^2/2\le9/(2\varepsilon)$. Since the middle quantity is $\tan\varphi(\tau_m)$ for the reference angle, this places the peak-angle cosine at the scale of $\varepsilon$. The formal statement gives only the displayed tangent bounds, with the time interval as a hypothesis. It does not establish that $\tau_m$ is a zero of $Y$ or an amplitude maximum; those facts come from Lemma 2.5.
notes.TorusEuler.ReferenceRiccati.x_mul_s_lt_o: For arbitrary real $\varepsilon,\tau$, put $x=\varepsilon\tau^2/2$ and $s=(1+x^2)^{-1/2}$. The formal statement proves $xs<1$. notes.TorusEuler.ReferenceRiccati.x_mul_s_sq_l: Let $x=\varepsilon\tau^2/2$ and $s=(1+x^2)^{-1/2}$. For all real $\varepsilon,\tau$, the formal statement proves $xs^2\le1/2$. notes.TorusEuler.ScheduledEulerConstruction.Po: At a selected child step let $\mu=\lambda_{j-1}$, $\lambda=\lambda_j$, and $T=S_j$. notes.TorusEuler.ScheduledEulerConstruction.Sc: For a selected depth-$P$ expansion on $[0,T]$, this condition prescribes factorially weighted time bounds through order $q$. notes.TorusEuler.ScheduledEulerConstruction.ex: Choose the integer envelope exponent $a$ above a fixed threshold, independent of time order. Given parent coefficient bounds through time order $q+1$, with the residual through order $q$, the formal statement bounds the selected mean for every phase-independent source $f_{\rm m}$ by $\mathcal J_{q+1}(B)_{[m]}\le K_m\mathsf D^{r_0+a}\mathcal J_q(f_{\rm m})_{[m+1]}$. Fix nonnegative integers $q,A$. Before choosing a construction or stage, the formal statement selects an integer $E$ and nonnegative constants $C_m$. atural$ for the approximate velocity before truncation, $O_j=W_{m osc}^

notes.TorusEuler.SpatiallyPeriodic: A field on $\mathbb R^3$ is spatially periodic when $f(x+n)=f(x)$ for every $x\in\mathbb R^3$ and every $n\in\mathbb Z^3$. The formal condition allows any target space, so the same convention applies to velocity, pressure and other fields. It represents a field on $\mathbb T^3=\mathbb R^3/\mathbb Z^3$, with opposite faces of the centered cube identified. Periodicity alone imposes no continuity, differentiability, parity, incompressibility or mean-zero condition. These must be stated separately. In particular, a real wave vector in an unlocalized periodic profile does not automatically produce such a field.
notes.TorusEuler.TruncatedChildStage: A truncated stage supplies continuous torus representatives of $V$ and $R_V$, a velocity $u=S_\Lambda V$, and a smooth periodic pressure $p$ of zero spatial mean on $[0,T]$. It requires $u$ smooth, odd and divergence free, with Fourier support $|\xi|\le2\Lambda$, and $\Delta p=-\operatorname{tr}((\nabla u)^2)$. Its actual momentum residual is identified both with $u_t+\mathbb P\operatorname{div}(u\otimes u)$ and with the cutoff expression in (5.58). These are conditions on the supplied objects, not an existence proof. A separate theorem constructs them from an approximate solution. No vanishing residual or quantitative cutoff error is part of this declaration.
notes.TorusEuler.TruncatedChildStage.pressureH: Let $p,q$ be smooth periodic scalar functions on $\mathbb R^3$ and suppose $\|D^2(p-q)\|_{C^{0,1/2}}\le B$. Then at every point and for every vector $v$, $v\cdot D^2p\,v\le v\cdot D^2q\,v+B|v|^2$. Thus $D^2p\le D^2q+BI$ as quadratic forms. Periodicity ensures the relevant Hölder norm is finite. This is the passage used in §5.7 to add the cutoff pressure error to the upper bound for the approximate pressure. The statement does not itself bound $D^2q$, choose either pressure, or assert a two-sided bound on $D^2p$.
notes.TorusEuler.TruncatedChildStage.residual: For the truncated velocity $u$ and its smooth periodic zero-mean Poisson pressure $p$, define $R_u(t,x)=\partial_tu(t,x)+(u(t,x)\cdot\nabla)u(t,x)+\nabla p(t,x)$. The time derivative is taken within $[0,T]$, so the values at $0$ and $T$ use one-sided derivatives on that interval. This is the residual in Proposition 5.11. The same chosen fields carry identities expressing it through the Leray projection and cutoff tensors. The definition alone does not assert $R_u=0$, a norm bound, or a Fourier support bound; those are separate properties or estimates of the truncated stage.
notes.TorusEuler.TruncatedChildStage.slabTimeJ: Let $T>0$, $\lambda\ge2$, and let $V$ be smooth and periodic on the closed slab. Use the fixed cutoff of the selected construction at $\Lambda=\lambda^5$. At a given time, assume $\|\partial_t^iV\|_{C^{0,1/2}}\le\lambda^{2+\psi}$ and that one plus the order-zero cutoff constant is at most $\lambda$. The formal statement proves $|\partial_t^i(S_\Lambda V)(t,x)|\le\lambda^{\psi+3}$ for every $x$. The exponent $\psi$ may be any real number. Endpoint derivatives are taken within the slab. This is the velocity estimate used to finish auxiliary Lemma 1.3, conditional on the approximate-velocity bound; it does not establish the residual estimate.

Let $V=U+O+M$ on $[0,T]$, where $T>0$, $V$ is smooth and periodic, and $M$ is smooth. Use the selected cutoff at $\Lambda=\lambda^5$, with $\lambda\ge2$. Fix integers $q,m,P$ with $m\le P$, and assume $5m+5+\psi\le3P$, the order-$P$ cutoff constant is at most $\lambda$, and $\|\partial_t^qV\|_{C^{P,1/2}}\le\lambda^{2(P+1)+\psi}$. If $\partial_t^qM$ has finite spatial Hölder norm at most $\tfrac12\lambda^{-1}$, the formal statement proves finiteness and the bound $\|\partial_t^q(S_\Lambda V-U-O)\|_{C^{m,1/2}}\le\lambda^{-1}$. This is a pointwise-in-time estimate on the closed slab. Continuity in the spatial norm is a separate assertion in the full auxiliary lemma.

Let $V,R_V$ be smooth on a positive closed time slab and let every time derivative have the specified continuous periodic representative. Fix a spatial cutoff $S_\Lambda$ independent of time. The formal statement gives $\partial_t^qR_j=\mathbb P[S_\Lambda\partial_t^qR_V+\operatorname{div}\sum_{i=0}^q\binom qi E_\Lambda(\partial_t^iV,\partial_t^{q-i}V)]$, where $E_\Lambda(f,g)=(S_\Lambda f)\otimes(S_\Lambda g)-S_\Lambda(f\otimes g)$. Time derivatives fix the physical point and are taken within the slab. This formula includes all nonnegative orders, and at order zero its tensor difference rearranges into the three terms displayed in the auxiliary note. It is an identity, not a bound on the residual. The theorem does not assume that the cutoff commutes with an arbitrary time-dependent symbol.

Let $V$ be smooth on $[0,T]\times\mathbb R^3$, with $T>0$, and suppose each time derivative is represented by the specified continuous field on $\mathbb R^3/\mathbb Z^3$. For a fixed cutoff symbol and fixed scale $\Lambda$, the formal statement proves $\partial_t^q(S_\Lambda V)=S_\Lambda(\partial_t^qV)$ at every time of the closed interval and every spatial point. The paper writes the corresponding identity for $(S_\Lambda-\operatorname{Id})V$; that form also requires subtracting $\partial_t^qV$. No estimate or Fourier-tail decay is part of this identity.

Let $V$ be smooth and periodic on $[0,T]\times\mathbb R^3$, with $T>0$, and use the fixed cutoff of the selected construction at any scale $\Lambda>0$. The formal Hölder-norm definition is omitted; the displayed interpretation follows the accompanying paper vocabulary.
notes.TorusEuler.abs_fixedOrderCost_le_thresho: Let $c_k(m,p)$ be any finite family of real numbers depending on nonnegative integer derivative order $m$ and expansion depth $p$. Put $K(s)=320b(s+1)$ and let $\mathcal B(s)$ be the maximum of $e^{4K(s+1)^3}$ and the sum of $|c_k(m,p)|$ over all indices with $m,p\le7K(s)$. The formal theorem proves $|c_k(m,p)|\le\mathcal B(s)$ for every entry in those ranges. No positivity or monotonicity of the cost table is assumed. This gives the arithmetic domination used in §1.5, including order and depth zero. Identification of the table entries with the paper’s analytic estimates remains a separate requirement.
notes.TorusEuler.activationGrowthRate_bounds: Let $\mu>0$, $L\ge0$, and let $c,C>0$ satisfy $c\mu^{1/4}\le\sigma\le C\mu^{1/4}L^2$ and $\pi\le\nu\le4\pi$. The formal statement proves $\sqrt{2c\pi}\,\mu^{1/8}\le r\le\sqrt{8C\pi}\,\mu^{1/8}L$, where $r=\sqrt{2\sigma\nu}$. Thus the unspecified constants in the growth-rate bound of §7.2 can be expressed in terms of the constants in the strength bounds. This is an inequality for positive real parameters; it does not establish that a particular wave has those strength and coupling bounds. Those must already be supplied at activation.
notes.TorusEuler.activationTimes_converge: Let $t_j$ be real times with $t_0\ge0$, and let $\tau_j>0$ satisfy $4\tau_{j+1}\le\tau_j$. Assume $0\le t_{j+1}-t_j\le\tau_j$ and that, after every index $j$, some time is strictly larger than $t_j$. Then there is $T_\infty>0$ with $t_j\to T_\infty$, $0<T_\infty-t_j\le4\tau_j/3$ and $T_\infty<t_j+2\tau_j$ for every $j$. Strict increase at every step is not required; the last hypothesis excludes an eventually constant sequence. The statement is an abstract result about times and needs no Euler fields. The explicit comparison with $\sum_{p\ge j}\tau_p$ occurs in the proof, not in its conclusion.
notes.TorusEuler.affineWaveAmplitudeOperator: For a bounded linear map $D$ on a real inner-product space and a vector $k$, the formal operator is $\mathbf a\mapsto-D\mathbf a+2(k\cdot D\mathbf a)k/|k|^2$. Its specialization to Euclidean $\mathbb R^3$ is the amplitude equation (2.1). Linearity in $\mathbf a$ is built into this expression and is used for nonvanishing and propagation. No hypothesis $k\ne0$ is imposed by the definition: division by zero is assigned zero, so at $k=0$ the operator is $-D$. Continuity as a function of a varying $k$ requires separate hypotheses; the physical wave arguments use a nonvanishing wave vector.
notes.TorusEuler.affineWaveAmplitudeOperator_a: All vectors lie in a real inner-product space. At $\kappa=0$, the inverse squared norm is assigned zero, so the identity remains algebraically meaningful. Substituting the pressure slope from (5.16) turns the projected equation (5.17) into the transverse momentum equation (5.15). This is a pointwise algebraic identity in $M$, $\kappa$, $f$ and $V$. It permits either form of the equation in the argument, but does not itself construct a solution or establish its time evolution.

For any bounded linear map $D$ and vectors $k,\mathbf a$ in a real inner-product space, the formal identity evaluates the amplitude operator as $-D\mathbf a+2(k\cdot D\mathbf a)k/|k|^2$. In $\mathbb R^3$ this is the second equation of (2.1); with $D=M$ and $k=\kappa$ it also supplies the right-hand side of (3.2) along a particle path. It is an algebraic identity, not existence of an amplitude solution. No nonzero or transversality hypothesis is required. When $k=0$, division by zero is assigned zero and both expressions reduce to $-D\mathbf a$.
notes.TorusEuler.affineWavePressure: At a fixed time, for a linear map $S$ on $\mathbb R^3$, scalar $p_{\rm w}$, vector $k$ and function $P$, the formal pressure is $p(x)=-x\cdot Sx/2-p_{\rm w}P(k\cdot x)$. It is a function on all of $\mathbb R^3$. In Lemma 2.1 one substitutes $S=D'+D^2$ and a primitive $P'=F$. Those identities and symmetry of $S$ are not imposed by the definition. Neither is periodicity or zero phase average of $P$. notes.TorusEuler.affineWavePressureCoeff: For a spatial linear map $D$ and vectors $k,\mathbf a\in\mathbb R^3$, the formal coefficient is $p_{\rm w}=2k\cdot D\mathbf a/|k|^2$, as in (1.4) and (2.1). For a nonzero wave vector satisfying the wave equations, substituting this coefficient gives $(k\cdot\mathbf a)'=0$; interval persistence of perpendicularity additionally uses an initial zero pairing.
notes.TorusEuler.affineWaveVelocity: For arbitrary time-dependent $D,k,\mathbf a$ and scalar profile $F$, the formal velocity is $u(t,x)=D(t)x+F(k(t)\cdot x)\mathbf a(t)$ on $\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3$. It is the full velocity $Dx+w$ of §1.1, not merely the perturbation $w$. The definition imposes no differentiability, periodicity, transversality or Euler equation. In particular a nonzero linear background is generally not a periodic velocity on the torus. Lemma 2.1 obtains the Euler conclusion after imposing the background compatibility and wave equations, while the later construction localizes these waves to obtain periodic fields.
notes.TorusEuler.affineWave_materialAccelerati: At a space-time point, suppose $D,k,\mathbf a$ have time derivatives $D',k',\mathbf a'$ relative to a time set with unique derivatives, $k'=-D^Tk$, $k\cdot\mathbf a=0$, and $F$ is differentiable at $k\cdot x$. notes.TorusEuler.angularLeray: For a spatial frequency $\xi\in\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\}$, the symbol is $r(\xi)=I-\widehat\xi\otimes\widehat\xi$, where $\widehat\xi=\xi/|\xi|$. Thus it projects vectors orthogonally onto $\xi^\perp$. The formal definition assigns zero to the normalized vector at $\xi=0$, giving $r(0)=I$ rather than removing the spatial mean. This is the spatial symbol in Lemma A.2. In the time-path case it must be combined with the separate projection subtracting the time average.
notes.TorusEuler.angularLeray_zero: The spatial Leray symbol equals the identity at frequency zero. Its definition uses $I-\widehat\xi\otimes\widehat\xi$, with the normalized zero vector assigned value zero, so this conclusion includes the exceptional frequency explicitly. In Appendix A.1, a constant spatial vector field therefore survives the Leray projection. Subtracting the time mean is a different operation: the mixed endpoint projection also applies that time projection, even in the spatial zero mode.
notes.TorusEuler.appendixCoefficientMultiIndex: For a phase-independent coefficient $c:I\times\mathbb R^3\to A$ in a real normed algebra, this expression is $|c|_m=\sum_{|\beta|=m}\sup_{t,a}|\partial_a^\beta c(t,a)|$. notes.TorusEuler.auxiliaryLemma12: The formal theorem chooses an exponent parameter, a nondecreasing threshold $\mathcal B$, and $N_1$ such that every initial frequency $N\ge N_1$ admits a selected common construction with $\lambda_0=N$. In that one construction, every fixed pair $(m,q)$ eventually satisfies $\|\partial_t^q(U_j-U_{j-1}-O_j)\|_{C^{m,1/2}}\le\lambda_j^{-1}$ throughout $[0,S_j]$, and the differentiated correction is continuous in that spatial norm. The starting stage may depend on both orders and the construction. This is a proved selected-construction version of auxiliary Lemma 1.2. It does not quantify over all cutoff symbols, all admissible thresholds or all constructions having the Section 7 conclusions. The exact spatial-norm formula is not included in this packet.
notes.TorusEuler.auxiliaryLemma13: The formal theorem chooses an exponent parameter, a nondecreasing threshold and an initial-frequency lower bound before constructing the sequence. Every sufficiently large initial frequency then admits a selected construction in which each $q$ has an integer $\psi_q$ and a starting stage such that $|\partial_t^iU_j|\le\lambda_j^{\psi_q}$ and $|\partial_t^iR_j|\le\lambda_{j+1}^{-5/2}$ for all $i\le q$ and all later stages. Both time curves are continuous in the spatial supremum norm on $[0,S_j]$. This proves the stated time estimates with a more specific, nonnegative integer exponent. It is existential in the selected construction and does not prove the separate generalized assertion for every qualifying construction.
notes.TorusEuler.auxiliaryTerminalSmoothness: The theorem chooses an exponent $b$, a nondecreasing threshold $\mathcal B$ and a bound $N_1$ before the initial frequency $N$. For each $N\ge N_1$, it produces scheduled stages with time-derivative estimates, a finite positive accumulation time, and an odd smooth periodic Euler solution with every singularity conclusion of Theorem 1.1. That velocity has a periodic extension smooth for all real times away from the torus origin, without any post-terminal Euler requirement. The conclusion selects a threshold rather than quantifying over all admissible thresholds. It does not explicitly assert convergence of its selected stages to its selected solution; that stronger relation is not part of the displayed conclusion.
notes.TorusEuler.centeredCell: The formal domain is the closed cube $\{x\in\mathbb R^3:-1/2\le x_i\le1/2\text{ for }i=1,2,3\}$. Lebesgue integration over this cube defines the pressure normalization and the torus essential-supremum norms. The cube itself does not identify opposite faces; that identification is represented by imposing integer-translation invariance on the fields. Both boundary faces are included, but they have zero three-dimensional measure and therefore do not change these integrals or essential suprema. This is precisely the fundamental-cell convention in the introduction, not an additional boundary condition of vanishing velocity.
notes.TorusEuler.child_flow_scaled_gradient_le: Let $\mathsf D,\lambda\ge1$, let $a,c$ be nonnegative integers, and suppose $\ell_*^{-1}\le\mathsf D^a$ and $h=\lambda^{-1/2}$. If nonnegative quantities $A,B$ satisfy $A,B\le K\mathsf D^c\lambda^{-5/4}$, then $\ell_*^{-1}A+h^{-1}B\le2K\mathsf D^{a+c}\lambda^{-3/4}$. In Lemma 5.10 these quantities bound derivatives of the label velocity and its longitudinal component. The theorem is a scalar inequality: it does not prove the input derivative estimates or identify the left side with the actual gradient. Positivity of the physical radius is imposed elsewhere; the formal inequality only needs the displayed reciprocal bound.
notes.TorusEuler.child_flow_scaled_gradient_sm: Let $\mathsf D,\lambda\ge1$, $C,\delta\ge0$, and nonnegative integer exponents $p\le b$. Suppose $C\le\delta\Gamma_P$, $\Gamma_P\mathsf D^b\lambda^{-1/12}\le1$, and a quantity $G$ satisfies $G\le C\mathsf D^p\lambda^{-3/4}$. Then $G\le\delta$. This is the numerical absorption used before the Gronwall estimate in Lemma 5.10. It applies once $G$ has been identified with a bound for the scaled gradient; no differentiability or flow assertion is part of this lemma. The weaker frequency exponent $-1/12$ is sufficient because $\lambda\ge1$.
notes.TorusEuler.complexFrozenSymbols_fiveJets: Let $r(\xi)$ be a smooth family of orthogonal projections near a nonzero frequency, and let $B$ satisfy $\langle Bw,w\rangle\ge\mu\|w\|^2$ on each projected range, with $\mu>0$. If the derivatives of $r$ through order five satisfy $\|D^ir\|\le D^i$, $D\ge1$, put $Q=2+\mu^{-1}+\|B\|$ and $C=(5!)^2(2D)^5$. The complexified inverse of $rBr+I-r$ has derivatives through order five bounded by $CQ^{11}$; composing with $r$ changes this bound to $32D^5CQ^{11}$. These are the quantitative symbol estimates preceding (A.6), with the projection derivative bounds supplied as hypotheses.
notes.TorusEuler.complexifiedHalfHolderFourier: Let $H$ be a real Hilbert space, $B:H\to H$ bounded linear, and $v\in C^{0,1/2}(\mathbb T^3;H)$. For every spatial frequency $n\in\mathbb Z^3$, the formal statement gives $\widehat{Bv}(n)=B_{\mathbb C}\widehat v(n)$, where $B_{\mathbb C}$ is the extension of $B$ to the compatible complex space used for Fourier coefficients. The coefficient $B$ is independent of the spatial label. This includes $H=L^2([0,1];\mathbb R^3)$: $B$ may act on whole time paths while preserving each spatial Fourier mode. This establishes coefficient diagonalization after freezing. It does not identify the projection's symbol, invert a projected equation, or require coercivity.
notes.TorusEuler.contDiffOn_angularLeray: The map $\xi\mapsto I-\widehat\xi\otimes\widehat\xi$ is smooth on $\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\}$, and hence on the unit sphere used in Appendix A.1. The formal statement permits every differentiability order there. It makes no continuity or differentiability assertion at zero, where the symbol is separately defined to be the identity. This establishes the spatial part of the projection-symbol regularity; the projection on $L^2$ time paths also involves subtraction of the time mean.
notes.TorusEuler.contDiffOn_endpointFixedInver: Let $S(t)$ be a family of bounded linear isomorphisms of a real Banach space, whose forward operators vary with $C^n$ regularity on a prescribed set of times. Then $S(t)^{-1}$ varies with the same regularity in operator norm; $n$ may be finite or infinite. On a closed interval this uses derivatives from within that interval. Appendix A.2 applies the result after establishing invertibility of $S(t)v=\mathbb P(K(t)v)$ in a spatial norm. It neither proves that inverse exists nor supplies its coercivity estimate.
notes.TorusEuler.contDiffOn_endpointPrimitive_: If $T>0$ and $f:[0,T]\to E$ is $C^n$ in a real Banach space, for an integer $n\ge0$, then $Jf(t)=\int_0^tf(s)\,ds$ is $C^{n+1}$ on $[0,T]$. Differentiability at the endpoints is one-sided, so no smooth extension beyond the interval is required. In Appendix A.2 this applies to $f=\Omega v$ in a chosen spatial norm. It supplies the gain in time regularity; smoothness in space must be established independently.
notes.TorusEuler.contDiffOn_endpointVelocity_a: Let $T>0$, let $S(t)$ be smooth bounded isomorphisms of a real Banach space $X$, and let $P:E\to X$ be bounded linear. Assume $\Omega(t):X\to E$ and $L(t)\in E$ are smooth, $c\in X$ is constant, and continuous $v$ satisfies $S(t)v(t)=c+P J(\Omega v)(t)-P L(t)$ on $[0,T]$. Then $v$ and $Jv$ are smooth in time. This is the time bootstrap in Appendix A.2, applied after choosing a spatial norm. It does not by itself give spatial derivatives or pressure regularity. Here $Jw(t)=\int_0^tw(s)\,ds$.
notes.TorusEuler.contDiffOn_flatActivation_smu: Let $a<b$, let $\chi$ be a globally smooth real function with $\chi(t)=0$ for every $t\le a$, and let $g(t,x)$ be smooth on $[a,b]\times V$, with values in a normed space. The formal statement proves that $\chi(t)g(t,x)$ is smooth on $(-\infty,b]\times V$. Although $g$ is defined at earlier times, no regularity there is assumed: multiplication by zero removes those values. This supplies a gluing principle for the products after (3.7). The paper gives its cutoff only on $[0,T]$; this particular result requires a globally smooth extension of it.
notes.TorusEuler.contDiff_localizedTransported: Fix a time, a differentiability order $m$, and a map $A$. Suppose $A$ and the evaluated label field $a\mapsto f(t,a,k_*\cdot a)$ are $C^m$. Assume $0<\delta\le1/2$ and that this field vanishes whenever some coordinate satisfies $|a_i|>1/2-\delta$. Extending it periodically from the centered cell and composing with $A$ gives a $C^m$ field; the result includes $m=\infty$. The formal result imposes no lattice condition on $k_*\in\mathbb R^3$. The zero collar is the reason arbitrary phases can be extended without seams; periodicity of the resulting Eulerian field additionally requires the inverse map to commute with integer translations.
notes.TorusEuler.contDiff_waveSwitch: Let $\theta:\mathbb R\to[0,1]$ be the fixed smooth transition, equal to zero for arguments at most zero and one for arguments at least one. For any real activation time $t_0$ and rate $r$, the formal statement proves that $\widetilde\chi(t)=\theta(r(t-t_0))$ is smooth on $\mathbb R$. In particular there is no loss of regularity at the activation time or at the end of the switching interval. This conclusion does not require $r>0$. That positivity is needed separately to interpret the transition as switching on as time increases.
notes.TorusEuler.continuousOn_endpointFixedInv: Suppose $S(t)$ is a family of bounded linear isomorphisms of a Banach space and $t\mapsto S(t)$ is continuous in operator norm on a specified set of times. Then $t\mapsto S(t)^{-1}$ is continuous in the same norm. The interval may be closed. In Appendix A.2 this applies to $S(t)v=\mathbb P(K(t)v)$ on solenoidal $C^{0,1/2}$ fields. Existence of the isomorphisms and their uniform bounds are premises, obtained separately from ellipticity and Lemma A.2.
notes.TorusEuler.continuous_and_norm_sub_le_en: Let $w$ be a spatially half-Hölder field with values in $L^2([0,T];E)$. Its primitive $Jw(t)$ is continuous in the spatial $C^{0,1/2}$ norm and satisfies $\|Jw(t)-Jw(s)\|_{C^{0,1/2}}\le|t-s|^{1/2}\|w\|_{C^{0,1/2}(L^2)}$ for $s,t\in[0,T]$. The half-Hölder norm is the maximum of supremum and seminorm. The formal statement allows an arbitrary metric label space, including the unit torus. Applied to $w=\Omega v$, this makes the right side of (A.9) continuous before continuity of $v$ has been recovered. Here $Jw(t)=\int_0^tw(s)\,ds$.
notes.TorusEuler.coordinateCurl_rankOne: Let $\mathbf a,\kappa\in\mathbb R^3$ and let $D$ be the linear map $v\mapsto(\kappa\cdot v)\mathbf a$, the convention for $\mathbf a\otimes\kappa$. Forming the coordinate curl from this derivative matrix gives $\kappa\times\mathbf a$, with the usual orientation of the coordinate basis. No differentiability assertion about a velocity is needed for this algebraic identity; no orthogonality or nonzero-vector assumptions are required. When $D$ is a contribution to $\nabla U_j(t,0)$, the identity gives exactly the contribution to vorticity used in Proposition 8.2. It fixes both the tensor order and the cross-product sign.
notes.TorusEuler.couplingRatioOfGain_step: Let $L>0$ and $L_+\ge640L$, and set $\varepsilon=L^{-2}$ and $\varepsilon_+=L_+^{-2}$. The formal statement gives $\varepsilon_+=(L/L_+)^2\varepsilon\le\varepsilon/32$, together with $(\varepsilon\varepsilon_+)^{-1/2}=LL_+\le L_+^2$. For step $j$, take $L=L_j$ and $L_+=L_{j+1}$; then these are the ratio estimate (7.9) and the following comparison of crossing times. Both gains and both ratios are positive under the hypotheses, so inverse squares and the negative half-power have their ordinary meanings. The statement assumes the gain separation; it does not prove it from the frequency recurrence.
notes.TorusEuler.crossingClock_le_endpointHalf: Suppose $\mu,c,L>0$, $L_+\ge640L$, $r\ge c\mu^{1/8}$ and $L_+\ge2/c$. Define $\varepsilon=L^{-2}$, $\varepsilon_+=L_+^{-2}$ and $\tau=\mu^{-1/8}L_+^3$. The formal theorem proves $2(\varepsilon\varepsilon_+)^{-1/2}/r\le\tau$. With $L=L_j$ and $L_+=L_{j+1}$, the left side is the physical duration corresponding to the upper end of the crossing bracket, while $\tau=\tau_j$. This places any crossing already known to lie in that bracket before $t_j+\tau_j$. The theorem neither constructs a crossing nor states the intermediate bound by a constant times $\mu^{-1/8}L_{j+1}^2$.
