The full quadratic sum splits exactly into the interactions at levels two through $P$ and the remaining tail. The same identity treats label and phase derivatives with their respective level conventions. In Proposition 5.4 the first group cancels against the solved equations, leaving the two quadratic sums in (5.30).
notes.TorusEuler.hierarchy_completion_previous: For an integer $p\ge1$, the formal statement proves that the exponent of the correction generated by level $p-1$ is the oscillatory exponent at level $p$ minus $1/3$. In paper notation this says that $C_p$, inherited from $V_{p-1}$, fits at level $p$ with an additional factor $\lambda^{-1/3}$. The oscillatory exponent is $-5/4-2(p-1)/3$, and a correction subtracts one further power from the generating oscillation. The assumption $p\ge1$ prevents truncation in the nonnegative-integer index $p-1$. This is arithmetic among assigned exponents; an estimate for the actual correction requires the analytic bounds.
notes.TorusEuler.hierarchy_fast_completion_exp: Here $i\ge1$ is assumed before forming the predecessor $i-1$, so the natural-number subtraction equals ordinary integer subtraction; the physical correction interactions have $i\ge2$. For an interaction with $i+j=p+1$, the phase cost $\lambda^{3/2}$ combined with $C_i$ and $Y_j$ leaves an extra factor $\lambda^{-1/12}$ beyond the target level-$p$ oscillatory bound. This is the weakest surplus in the induction for Theorem 5.6 and determines the frequency smallness needed to absorb the parent powers.
notes.TorusEuler.hierarchy_fast_mean_exponent: This is a numerical identity for nonnegative indices; all frequency exponents use real subtraction, and it asserts no bound for a profile by itself. When $i+j=p+1$, the induction bound for $B_i$, the oscillatory bound for $Y_j$, and one fast derivative give the target level-$p$ exponent with an extra $\lambda^{-1/4}$. This includes the term involving $B_p$ and $V_1$. It is the frequency calculation used for $f_p^S$ near the end of the induction.
notes.TorusEuler.hierarchy_label_product_expon: This equality is valid for all nonnegative integer indices, since those indices are treated as real numbers inside the exponents. Adding the oscillatory frequency exponents at levels $i$ and $j$ gives the mean exponent at level $i+j$. It also leaves a surplus $\lambda^{-7/12}$ relative to the oscillatory target at that level. This arithmetic supplies the power used for label-advection products in the proof of Theorem 5.6 after applying (5.39).
notes.TorusEuler.hierarchy_level_bounds: Assume nonnegative measured quantities obey the stated recurrence, $\lambda,L,K\ge1$, and $L^6\lambda^{-1/12}\le1$, at finite depth $P$. The numerical recurrence gives the source, velocity, mean, and correction estimates under its frequency smallness condition. An order-$n$ estimate at level $p$ requires the recurrence through order $n+3(p-1)+1$. Theorem 5.6 supplies these higher orders simultaneously. In particular, the propagated oscillatory source and induction mean bounds contain no remaining parent factor.
notes.TorusEuler.hierarchy_mean_inductive_shif: Explicitly, $[-5/2-2(p-2)/3]+1/12=-7/4-2(p-1)/3$ for every nonnegative integer $p$, with real subtraction throughout. The exponent in the sharper mean estimate (5.35), increased by $1/12$, equals the mean exponent used in (5.40). Thus replacing a parent factor by $\lambda^{1/12}$ gives exactly the induction bound stated in the paper. This is an algebraic identity; the actual mean estimate is supplied by the endpoint solve.
notes.TorusEuler.hierarchy_mean_product_expone: Explicitly, adding $-7/4-2(i-1)/3$ and $-7/4-2(j-1)/3$ gives $-5/2-2(i+j-2)/3-1$. The equality itself needs no flow or solution. Adding the induction exponents for two means gives the mean exponent at their combined level minus one. Once the label-advection estimate is applied, their product is therefore smaller by $\lambda^{-1}$ than the leading averaged oscillatory terms. This is the comparison of the third sum with the first two sums after (5.42).
notes.TorusEuler.hierarchy_phaseMean_supplemen: Fix vectors $B$ and $\kappa$ independent of phase. Let $Y(s)$ have period one, and suppose $Y'(s)$ exists for every phase and is continuous. The formal statement proves $\int_0^1(B\cdot\kappa)Y'(s)\,ds=0$. The endpoint values cancel by periodicity. At each fixed time and label this is the average cancellation for the supplementary term $(B_2\cdot\kappa)\partial_s(\widetilde\chi A_1)$ in (1.12). No zero-mean assumption on $Y$ is needed, and no amplitude or derivative estimate is concluded. The result uses phase independence of $B,\kappa$; it would not apply to arbitrary phase-dependent factors.
notes.TorusEuler.higherPressureGradientBudget_: Let $\lambda\ge1$ and $\alpha_p=-5/4-2(p-1)/3$. Suppose for $2\le p\le P$ that $F_p\le C\lambda^{\alpha_p}$, $V_p\le CL\lambda^{\alpha_p}$, $\lambda q_p\le CL\lambda^{\alpha_p}$ with $q_p\ge0$, and $g_p\le c_FF_p+c_VV_p+c_qq_p$. Assume $C,L,c_F,c_V,c_S\ge0$ and $c_q\le c_S\lambda$. Then $\sum_{p=2}^{P}g_p\le(P-1)C[c_F+(c_V+c_S)L]\lambda^{-23/12}$ for $P\ge2$; when the index set is empty the bound is zero. This is the numerical summation used before (5.52). Identifying these scalar quantities with pressure-gradient, source and velocity norms requires the preceding analytic estimates.
notes.TorusEuler.inductionPressure_endpointHes: Let $u$ be jointly $C^2$ on $[0,T]\times\mathbb R^3$, with $T>0$, and let $X$ satisfy $\dot X=u(t,X)$ at the time considered. Assume $D_x^2p$ exists there, $\lambda_0\ge4$, $\lambda_{n+1}\ge2\lambda_n$, and $D_x^2p(t,X)\le(\sum_{i<j}\lambda_i^{-1})I$. If the spatial derivative of the momentum residual has operator norm at most $1/2$, the formal theorem gives $H\le I$ for $H=-\dot A-A^2$, $A=D_xu(t,X)$. The frequency assumptions bound the reciprocal sum by $1/2$. This is a local bound along the indicated trajectory and time; it does not assume that the approximate parent solves Euler exactly or assert an endpoint inverse by itself.
notes.TorusEuler.inductionPressure_sum_le: Let $\lambda_0>0$ and suppose $2\lambda_i\le\lambda_{i+1}$ for every nonnegative integer $i$. For every $j\ge0$, the formal statement proves $\sum_{i=0}^{j-1}\lambda_i^{-1}\le2/\lambda_0$. This is the sum $\sum_{i=1}^{j}\lambda_{i-1}^{-1}$ appearing in (T3), written with indices starting at zero. When $j=0$ the sum is empty and equals zero. Positivity of every frequency follows from the hypotheses, so all reciprocals are ordinary positive reciprocals. The statement only bounds the numerical allowance; an estimate for the pressure Hessian must already have been established separately.
notes.TorusEuler.induction_child_center_error_: If $\lambda\ge2^{12}$ and $\lambda_+\ge\lambda$, then $\lambda^{-1/3}+\lambda_+^{-5}\le\lambda^{-1/4}$. The statement is a numerical estimate for positive real frequencies, with no gradient field among its data. In §7.2 the two summands bound the central error of the approximate solution and the derivative of the Fourier tail. Once their sum bounds $|E_{c,j}|$, this inequality gives the error allowance in (T4). The explicit threshold $2^{12}$ replaces the phrase “for large $N$” for this individual comparison; the construction still has other threshold requirements.
notes.TorusEuler.induction_child_velocity_boun: Let $\mu\ge2$, $\lambda\ge2\mu$ and let $U_+,U,O:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ satisfy $|U(x)|\le\mu$ and $|O(x)|\le\lambda^{-1}$. Assume $U_+-U-O$ has finite spatial $C^{0,1/2}$ norm at most $\lambda^{-1}$. Then $|U_+(x)|\le\lambda$ for every $x$. This proves the final velocity bound used in (T2), after the oscillation and remaining increment have been controlled. The formal statement is for a single spatial field and does not itself take a supremum in time. The intermediate triangle-inequality bound $\mu+2\lambda^{-1}$ is used in the proof. The exact Hölder norm normalization is not defined in the supplied packet.
notes.TorusEuler.induction_comparison_error_bu:
Let $\mu\ge1$, $
u\ge1$, $c,L>0$, $L_+\ge0$, $A\ge0$ and $r\ge c\mu^{1/8}$. Suppose $0\le B\le\mu^{1/32}$, $B_t\le\mu^{1/16}$ and $E\le\mu^{-1/4}$ are numerical bounds, and $\delta\le A[2\mu^{-1/8}L_+^3(B^2+B_t)/(
u L^{-2})+B/r+E/
u]$. The formal theorem concludes $\delta\le A(5+c^{-1})[L^2L_+^3\mu^{-1/16}+\mu^{-3/32}+\mu^{-1/4}]$. This is the substitution of the scheduled bounds into (6.6), with an explicit resulting constant. It assumes the initial comparison estimate and the older-gradient bounds; it does not establish them for an Euler construction. In the application $L=L_j$, $L_+=L_{j+1}$ and $L^2=\varepsilon^{-1}$.
notes.TorusEuler.induction_older_gradient_scal: Let $b\ge1$ and $q\ge0$ be integers, let $\lambda_{\rm old}\ge1$, and put $\mu=\lambda_{\rm old}^{320b(q+1)}$. If numerical bounds satisfy $B\le\lambda_{\rm old}^9$ and $B_t\le\lambda_{\rm old}^{18}$, then $B\le\mu^{1/32}$ and $B_t\le\mu^{1/16}$. In §7.2 the inputs are uniform norms of the gradient and its time derivative for the older velocity, with $\lambda_{\rm old}=\lambda_{j-2}$. This theorem supplies the change of frequency scale only. It neither produces those analytic derivative estimates nor assumes that $B,B_t$ are themselves functions or matrices.
notes.TorusEuler.inductive_oscillations_eventu: Let $K\subset\mathbb R^3\setminus\mathbb Z^3$ be compact. Suppose radii $r_n\to0$, and for every $0\le t\le T$, any point where $O_{n+1}(t)$ is nonzero lies within distance $r_n$ of an integer lattice point. Then there is an open neighbourhood $V$ of $K$, avoiding the lattice, and an index $N$ such that $O_{n+1}(t,x)=0$ for all $n\ge N$, $t\in[0,T]$ and $x\in V$. No smoothness is required for this support argument. In Proposition 8.4 the radii are $\lambda_n^{-1}$. Vanishing on a neighbourhood, uniformly in time, allows the spatial derivatives of the later oscillations to vanish near $K$ as well.

Assume $t_n\to T_\infty$ and $O_n(t,\cdot)=0$ for every $n\ge2$ and $0\le t\le t_n$. For each fixed $S<T_\infty$, there is an index $N$ such that $O_{n+1}(t,x)=0$ for every $n\ge N$, $t\in[0,S]$ and $x\in\mathbb R^3$. Neither monotonicity of the activation sequence nor smoothness of the fields is needed for this assertion. Proposition 8.1 combines this eventual vanishing with the correction estimates to obtain convergence in higher spatial norms. The formal statement supplies some sufficiently large index; it does not identify that index with the particular $j_0$ chosen in the paper to control both time and derivative order.
notes.TorusEuler.inner_normalize_cross3_left: For $\kappa,\mathbf a\in\mathbb R^3$, the scalar product of the normalized covector with $\kappa\times\mathbf a$ is zero. For a nonzero covector this reads $(\kappa/|\kappa|)\cdot(\kappa\times\mathbf a)=0$. The formal formula also permits $\kappa=0$, with normalization defined as zero there; it makes no unit-vector assertion in that case. Applied to the gradient contribution $\widetilde\chi_j\mathbf a_j\otimes\kappa_j$, the identity removes the newest wave from the projection used in Proposition 8.2, for any real cutoff value. It does not give a lower bound for the projection of the preceding wave; that requires the separate angle and strength estimates.
notes.TorusEuler.integral_endpointLabelEnergy_: On $[0,T]$, $T\ge0$, assume $F_t=MF$, $M_t$ is continuous, $z_t=v$ with continuous $v$, and $z(0)=z(T)=0$. Put $\xi=Fz$, $K=F^TF$, $\Omega=F^T(M^T-M)F$, and $H^\#=-(M_t+M^2)$. Then $\int_0^T(Kv\cdot v+\Omega v\cdot z)\,dt=\int_0^T(|\xi_t|^2-H^\#\xi\cdot\xi)\,dt$. This is (4.7) for continuously differentiable paths in a real Hilbert space. The extension to all $H^1_0$ displacements is not part of this statement and is needed separately for Lemma 4.1.
notes.TorusEuler.integral_endpointLabelVelocit: Let $0\le T\le1$, $F_t=MF$, $z_t=v$ with continuous $M,v$, and $z(T)=0$. Suppose $GF=I$, $\|G\|\le D$, $\|M\|\le L$, where $D,L\ge0$. Then, for $\xi=Fz$, $\int_0^T|v|^2\,dt\le D^2(1+L)^2\int_0^T|\xi_t|^2\,dt$. This gives the exact factor in (4.6) for continuously differentiable paths. It does not require $z(0)=0$, but it does require continuous $v$; the paper's complete $H^1_0$ assertion uses the separate square-integrable-velocity result.
notes.TorusEuler.integral_inner_gradient_cente: Let $w:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ and $q:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R$ be $C^1$ and invariant under integer translations, and suppose $\operatorname{div}w=0$ everywhere. The formal theorem proves $\int_{[-1/2,1/2]^3}w\cdot\nabla q\,dx=0$. Opposite faces cancel in integration by parts. No mean-zero assumption on $q$ is needed for this cancellation. The result supplies the spatial pressure cancellation used in the endpoint energy argument, after the displacement constraint and the volume-preserving change of variables have been established. It does not itself prove that change of variables, the Jacobi equation, or the space-time identity (1.8).
notes.TorusEuler.integral_norm_iteratedFDeriv_: Let $K$ be a complex-valued Schwartz function on $\mathbb R^3$, let $\Lambda>0$, and set $K_\Lambda(y)=\Lambda^3K(\Lambda y)$. For any $m\ge0$ and any fixed vectors $v_1,\ldots,v_m$, the formal statement proves $\int|D^mK_\Lambda(y)[v_1,\ldots,v_m]|\,dy=\Lambda^m\int|D^mK(y)[v_1,\ldots,v_m]|\,dy$. Taking coordinate directions and replacing $\Lambda$ by $4\Lambda$ gives the kernel identity used for (B.1). The scaling factor accounts for both differentiation and the three-dimensional change of variables. No cutoff symbol is assumed; rapid decay makes the integrals finite.
notes.TorusEuler.integral_norm_pow_scaledLiftK: Let $\Lambda>0$, $m\ge0$, and $K_\Lambda(y)=\Lambda^3K(\Lambda y)$ for $K:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb C$. The formal identity is $\int|y|^m|K_\Lambda(y)|\,dy=\Lambda^{-m}\int|y|^m|K(y)|\,dy$. It is stated for an arbitrary function $K$, with no integrability hypothesis, so its existence as an equality does not certify finite moments. For the Schwartz kernel $K=\check\psi$ in Appendix B, all these moments are finite and the identity has its usual integral meaning. It provides the factor $\Lambda^{s-M}$ after taking $m=M-s$ in the Taylor remainder estimate.
notes.TorusEuler.integral_scaledCutoffSchwartz: Suppose $\psi:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R$ is smooth and vanishes outside the ball of radius two, let $K=\check\psi$, and let $\Lambda>0$. The formal statement proves $\int_{\mathbb R^3}\Lambda^3K(\Lambda y)\,dy=\psi(0)$, with the right side viewed as a complex number. The kernel is Schwartz, so the integral is finite. Appendix B also assumes $\psi=1$ on the unit ball, which changes this right side to one. That plateau condition is not a hypothesis of this declaration; it must be supplied when reading the link as the paper's assertion of unit mass.

Let $\psi$ be smooth on $\mathbb R^3$, zero outside the radius-two ball and identically one on the unit ball. For $\Lambda>0$, set $K_\Lambda(y)=\Lambda^3\check\psi(\Lambda y)$. The formal statement proves $\int y_{i_1}\cdots y_{i_m}K_\Lambda(y)\,dy=0$ for every positive integer $m$ and every choice of coordinate indices, including repetitions. Thus it covers every positive-order multi-index moment used in Appendix B. The moment is the integral of the signed or complex kernel, not of its absolute value. No radiality or evenness is required for this cancellation.
notes.TorusEuler.inverseAdjoint_activationWave: Let $F:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ be any invertible linear map, $\lambda\in\mathbb R$ and $E_3\in\mathbb R^3$. The formal statement proves $F^{-T}(\lambda F^TE_3)=\lambda E_3$. In §6.2, take $F=D_aX(t_0,0)$ and choose $k_*=\lambda F^TE_3(t_0)$; then the transported covector at activation is exactly $\lambda E_3(t_0)$. The theorem is linear algebra and does not itself assert that $F$ is a flow derivative or that $E_3$ is a unit vector. It does not require integer components of $k_*$; periodicity of the localized field is a separate issue.
notes.TorusEuler.isEulerSolution_stationaryShe: For any real $\rho$ and any $T>0$, the formal theorem proves that $u(t,x)=\sin(2\pi x_2)(e_1+\rho e_3)$ with $p(t,x)=0$ is a smooth periodic Euler solution on $[0,T)$. The velocity varies only in $x_2$ and has zero second component, so both divergence and self-advection vanish. Pressure is automatically mean zero. This verifies the starting flow described in §1.1 and (6.1), under weaker assumptions on $\rho$: positivity and smallness are unnecessary for the stationary Euler identity. They are imposed later to obtain the positive couplings and separation used for amplification.
notes.TorusEuler.iteratedFDeriv_comp_sub_linea: Assume $n>0$, $f$ is $n$ times continuously differentiable at $g(x)$ and $g$ is $n$ times continuously differentiable at $x$. Derivatives are multilinear maps. The derivative of a composition, after subtracting the outer derivative applied to the highest inner derivative, is a sum indexed by partitions with at least two parts. Each term therefore involves lower-order inner derivatives. In Proposition 5.1, taking the composition $U\circ X$ produces the forcing $N_\beta$ in the higher variational equation.
notes.TorusEuler.kineticForm: For a bounded linear operator $F$ on a real Hilbert space, define $K=F^*F$. Thus $\langle Kv,v\rangle=\|Fv\|^2$, so $K$ is nonnegative. For Euclidean particle labels the adjoint is the matrix transpose, and $F=D_aX$ gives $K=(D_aX)^TD_aX$ in (4.1). The definition imposes no invertibility or flow equation on $F$. A positive lower bound for $K$ requires a separate estimate on a left inverse of $F$.
notes.TorusEuler.kineticForm_elliptic: Let $F,G$ be bounded operators on a real Hilbert space, with $GF=I$ and $\|G\|\le D$, where $D>0$. Then $\langle F^*Fv,v\rangle\ge D^{-2}\|v\|^2$ for every vector $v$. For $F=D_aX$ this is the ellipticity $K\ge D_-^{-2}I$ used in Theorem 4.2. Only a left inverse is needed. No bound on $F$ itself, symmetry of the velocity gradient, incompressibility or particle-flow equation is required for this linear-algebraic conclusion.
notes.TorusEuler.labelFlow_firstVariation: On $[l,r]$, suppose flows exist for every velocity $u+\varepsilon b$ with the same starting position $a$. Assume $u$ is spatially differentiable and uniformly Lipschitz, its spatial derivative is uniformly Lipschitz, and $b$ is jointly continuous, uniformly bounded and uniformly Lipschitz in space. Also require continuity of $D_xu$ along the unperturbed trajectory. Then the derivative of the perturbed flow at $\varepsilon=0$ exists at every time and is a path $\xi$ satisfying $\xi(l)=0$ and $\xi_t=D_xu(t,X(t,a))\xi+b(t,X(t,a))$. This establishes the actual first variation used in §4.1, not merely existence of a solution to its linear equation.
notes.TorusEuler.labelWaveVector: For a particle at $a$ at time $s$, the formal definition is $\kappa(t)=(D_xX(t,s)|_{X(s,t,a)})^Tk_*$. It differentiates the reverse map at the current particle position. When $X$ is the smooth parent flow, this equals $(D_aX(s,t,a))^{-T}k_*$; the paper uses $s=0$. The transpose is with respect to the Euclidean inner product. The formula accepts arbitrary maps and initial covectors, so nonvanishing and inverse identities are not automatic. Derivatives are assigned zero where they do not exist; the smooth-flow hypotheses and $k_*\ne0$ give the intended nondegenerate covector.
notes.TorusEuler.lemma31_waveProfile: The formal theorem proves the full conclusion of Lemma 3.1 for the specified families $F_h,P_h$. For $0<h\le1$, both are smooth and period one, $F_h$ is odd, $P_h'=F_h$, and $P_h$ has zero average over one phase period. One positive $C$ gives $F_h'(0)=1$, $-Ch\le F_h'\le1$ and $|F_h|\le Ch$ for all widths and phases. Each integer $j\ge2$ has its own positive width-independent $C_j$ with $|\partial_s^jF_h|\le C_jh^{1-j}$. The exponent is integral, preserving negative powers. The conclusion gives particular witnesses for the paper's existence claim; no properties are asserted for widths outside $(0,1]$.
notes.TorusEuler.liftConvolution_cutoffSchwart: Let $g$ be continuous on $\mathbb T^3=\mathbb R^3/\mathbb Z^3$ with values in a complex Banach space. Assume $\psi$ is smooth and zero outside the radius-two ball, and let $\Lambda>0$. For the periodic lift $f$ and $K_\Lambda(y)=\Lambda^3\check\psi(\Lambda y)$, the formal statement proves $(S_\Lambda g)(x)=\int_{\mathbb R^3}K_\Lambda(y)f(x-y)\,dy$. The field is bounded by compactness and the kernel is integrable. This is the representation used in Appendix B. No plateau, radiality or evenness is needed, but this particular result assumes a continuous complex-valued or complex Banach-valued field, not an arbitrary measurable real velocity.
notes.TorusEuler.linearODE_ne_zero_of_mem: Let $J$ be an interval, let $A(t)$ be continuous in operator norm on $J$, and let $x$ solve $x'=A(t)x$ there, with derivatives relative to $J$. The formal statement proves that $x(t_0)\ne0$ at one $t_0\in J$ implies $x(t)\ne0$ for every $t\in J$, both before and after $t_0$. It holds in any real normed vector space for bounded linear coefficients; no existence of a solution is asserted. In Lemma 2.1 it is applied separately to the wave-vector and amplitude equations, after verifying continuity of their coefficients.
notes.TorusEuler.linearODE_variation_of_consta: In a real Banach space, let $A$ and $f$ be continuous on $[a,b]$. Suppose bounded linear maps $\Phi,\Psi$ satisfy $\Phi(a)=\Psi(a)=I$, $\Phi\prime=A\Phi$ and $\Psi\prime=-\Psi A$, and let $z\prime=Az+f$ on the interval. Then $z(t)=\Phi(t)z(a)+\int_a^t\Phi(t)\Psi(r)f(r)\,dr$ for every $t\in[a,b]$. Derivatives at the endpoints are taken within the interval. The paper applies this general identity with the unperturbed triangular flow and forcing equal to the coefficient error applied to the perturbed solution. The statement assumes the two fundamental evolutions; it supplies neither their existence nor a propagator bound.
notes.TorusEuler.localizedCoefficient_holderHa: Suppose $r>0$, $0\le\chi\le1$, $\chi$ vanishes beyond distance $2r$ from $a_0$, and $|\chi(a)-\chi(b)|\le(C/r)d(a,b)$ with $C\ge0$. If $B$ has Lipschitz constant $L\ge0$, then $E(a)=\chi(a)(B(a_0)-B(a))$ satisfies $\|E\|_\infty\le2rL$, Lipschitz bound $(1+2C)L$, and half-Hölder seminorm at most $\max(4,1+2C)L\sqrt r$. These are the quantitative estimates used near the freezing point. For a full half-Hölder norm bound one must combine the supremum and increment estimates, using the small radius chosen in the proof.
notes.TorusEuler.localizedCompletedWave_proper: Fix a time. Let the smooth inverse label map commute with integer translations, and let a transverse profile vanish for all phases in a collar of the centered label-cell boundary. Assume its phase potential is jointly smooth in label and phase; inside the cell the covector must be nonzero and equal to $(D_xA)^Tk_*$. The formal statement constructs $W$ as the curl of the periodically extended evaluated potential. It proves that $W$ is smooth, spatially periodic and divergence free everywhere, and equals $V^\natural+C[V]^\natural$ where the label lies inside the cell. Arbitrary real $k_*$ are permitted. This is a spatial assertion at a fixed time; joint time regularity requires separate hypotheses.
notes.TorusEuler.localizedTransportedProfile: For an arbitrary real wave vector $k_*$, first evaluate the profile as $a\mapsto f(t,a,k_*\cdot a)$ on the centered label cell. The formal definition extends that field periodically and composes it with the inverse label map $A(t,x)$. This is the localized interpretation of $f^\natural$ in §3.1. It is a formula defined without smoothness or support assumptions. Vanishing near the cell boundary is needed for a smooth extension, and integer-translation equivariance of $A$ is needed for spatial periodicity after composition. The phase itself need not be periodic, and $k_*$ need not lie in $\mathbb Z^3$.
notes.TorusEuler.logNormDerivOfScaled: Let $v$ be a path in a real inner-product space and assume $v\ne0$ at a time where its relative derivative is $v'=|v|w$. The formal statement proves $(\log|v|)'=(v/|v|)\cdot w$. Substitution of $w=v'/|v|$ gives the logarithmic-norm identity displayed in the proof of Lemma 2.2. It applies to any such path, rather than only to the wave vector or amplitude. The norm is positive under the hypothesis, so the logarithm and division have their ordinary mathematical meanings. The wave equations must be substituted separately to obtain $-B_{11}$ and $-B_{22}$.
notes.TorusEuler.meanScalarBudget_le_power: Assume $\mathsf D\ge1$, nonnegative inverse, coefficient and source bounds, and $A_{\rm inv}\le C\mathsf D^a$. The estimate yields exponent $a+2b+2s$, deliberately enlarging the square-root costs. With $\ell_*=\mathsf D^{-s}$, the inverse estimate, two deformation factors and the Hölder comparison costs can be bounded by a single power of $\mathsf D$. The exponent may depend on the fixed radius exponent $s$. It does not depend on the derivative order, which is the essential requirement in Proposition 5.2.
notes.TorusEuler.meanScalarRadius_absorbs_inve: The exponents $a,s$ are nonnegative integers and $\mathsf D\ge1$, so $\ell_*>0$ and its square root has the usual positive meaning. If the inverse constant satisfies $A\le\mathsf D^a$ and $\ell_*=\mathsf D^{-s}$ with $s\ge2(a+9)$, then $A\mathsf D^9\sqrt{\ell_*}\le1$. This is the scalar smallness condition behind (5.13). The radius is chosen once from the inverse bound, rather than decreased separately at each derivative order.
notes.TorusEuler.momentumResidual: For a time set $I$, velocity $U$ and pressure $p$, the formal definition is $R_U=\partial_tU+(U\cdot\nabla)U+\nabla p$, with the time derivative taken within $I$. For a smooth parent on $[0,T]$, this is the ordinary material acceleration plus the pressure gradient, with one-sided derivatives at the endpoints. It is not an independent force chosen to fit an estimate. The definition does not impose $\operatorname{div}U=0$ or $R_U=0$, and derivative values outside their regularity hypotheses carry no Euler interpretation. In §1.3, the mean correction cancels this parent's defect together with the averaged wave error.
notes.TorusEuler.nonempty_truncatedChildStage:
Let $T>0$ and let $V,R_V$ be smooth periodic fields on $[0,T]	imes\mathbb R^3$, with $V$ odd and divergence free. Suppose a smooth periodic spatial pressure $\Pi(t)$ satisfies $V_t+V\cdot
abla V+
abla\Pi=R_V$ at every time, using time derivatives within the interval. For an even cutoff symbol, the formal construction produces the finite Fourier cutoff $u=S_\Lambda V$, a jointly smooth periodic zero-mean pressure with $\Delta p=-\operatorname{tr}((
abla u)^2)$, and the exact projected residual identity (5.58). The resulting velocity is smooth, odd, divergence free and supported in $|\xi|\le2\Lambda$. The construction does not require the symbol’s smooth tail estimates; those are additional inputs for the quantitative error bounds in Proposition 5.11.
notes.TorusEuler.norm_complexFrozenInverseSymb: Let $r$ be an orthogonal projection on a real Hilbert space and suppose $\langle Bw,w\rangle\ge\mu\|w\|^2$ on its range, with $\mu>0$. The inverse of $A=rBr+I-r$, extended to the compatible complex space used for Fourier coefficients, has operator norm at most $\min(1,\mu)^{-1}$. This is the Lax–Milgram bound invoked in Appendix A.1. It includes zero frequency if that projection satisfies the same assumptions. The statement establishes the bound at one frequency; differentiability in frequency and Hölder multiplier estimates are separate results.
notes.TorusEuler.norm_curlOfDerivative_ge_of_t: Suppose $D_{\rm mid}=D_{\rm old}+\mathbf a_p\otimes\kappa_p+E_p$ and $D_{\rm new}=D_{\rm mid}+\chi\mathbf a\otimes\kappa+E$, with $\kappa\ne0$. Assume $\|D_{\rm old}\|\le M$, $\|E_p\|\le e_p$, $\|E\|\le e$, and $(\kappa/|\kappa|)\cdot(\kappa_p\times\mathbf a_p)\ge b$. The formal statement gives $|\operatorname{curl}D_{\rm new}|\ge b-C(M+e_p+e)$, where curl of a matrix means its antisymmetric coordinate derivative combination, and $C$ is the norm of that fixed linear map. The tensor convention is $(\mathbf a\otimes\kappa)v=(\kappa\cdot v)\mathbf a$; $\chi$ may be any real number. This algebraic estimate does not contain the frequency powers in (8.2): their derivation requires substituting the induction bounds.
notes.TorusEuler.norm_iteratedFDeriv_labelJaco: This is a pointwise implication for a map $Y:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ at any natural order $n$; the stated bound for $D^{n+1}Y$ is a hypothesis. An order-$n$ derivative of $D_aX$ is controlled by the order-$(n+1)$ derivative of $X$. The flow bound $\mathsf D^{5(n+1)-4}$ therefore becomes $\mathsf D^{5n+1}$ for the deformation. This is the conversion immediately after the induction in Proposition 5.1, before the other coefficients are bounded by products and inverses.
notes.TorusEuler.norm_operatorLiftConvolution_: Let a smooth compactly supported operator-valued Fourier symbol vanish at zero, and let $G$ be its inverse Fourier kernel. Suppose a continuous bounded input satisfies $\|f(x)-f(y)\|\le H|x-y|^{1/2}$. At scale $\Lambda>0$, convolution with the rescaled kernel is bounded by $H\Lambda^{-1/2}\int\|G(y)\|\,|y|^{1/2}\,dy$. The zero value of the symbol gives the cancellation needed to subtract $f(x)$. Taking $\Lambda=2^j$ yields the half-power decay used in (A.6). The formal estimate leaves the kernel moment explicit; bounding it uniformly requires the preceding symbol estimates.
notes.TorusEuler.norm_phaseMean_le: Suppose $f:\mathbb R\to E$ takes values in a real normed space and $|f(s)|\le M$ for every $s\in[0,1]$. The formal statement proves $|\int_0^1f(s)\,ds|\le M$. The interval has length one, so no additional factor occurs. It neither assumes periodicity nor continuity. For the smooth finite-dimensional profiles of Appendix D, the integral is the usual phase average and this is its supremum contraction bound. For a general input, the statement does not prove integrability; that must be established independently when the integral is to represent an average.
notes.TorusEuler.norm_phasePrimitive_le: Let $f:\mathbb R\to E$ be continuous, one-periodic and of zero phase average, with $|f(s)|\le M$ on $[0,1]$. Its normalized primitive is $F(s)=\int_0^s f-\int_0^1\int_0^r f$. The formal statement proves $|F(s)|\le2M$ for every real $s$. The estimate is global in phase because zero average makes the primitive periodic. For the Banach or finite-dimensional targets used in the paper, it gives the zero-order primitive bound behind (D.5). This declaration estimates values only; commutation with label and phase derivatives is used separately to obtain the finite-order estimate.
notes.TorusEuler.norm_sq_mul_oscillatoryPressu: The slope is defined by $(\kappa\cdot f-2\kappa\cdot MV)/|\kappa|^2$; the nonzero hypothesis makes this ordinary division. For $\kappa\ne0$, the prescribed pressure slope obeys $\lVert\kappa\rVert^2\partial_s\mathsf p=\kappa\cdot f-2\kappa\cdot MV$, the identity (5.16). The result is algebraic and holds in a general real inner-product space. It determines the derivative in phase; taking the zero-mean primitive fixes the pressure itself.
notes.TorusEuler.norm_stationaryShearGradient_: For $B_\rho=2\pi(e_1+\rho e_3)\otimes e_2$, the formal statement proves $\|B_\rho\|\le4\pi$ whenever $|\rho|\le1$. This is the Euclidean operator norm: $B_\rho v=2\pi v_2(e_1+\rho e_3)$. The same matrix is $\nabla U_0(0)$ for $U_0(x)=\sin(2\pi x_2)(e_1+\rho e_3)$. The parameter range is larger than $0<\rho\le1$ in §6.1, since zero and negative tilts are allowed. There is no time or frequency hypothesis, and the estimate is not a statement about the gradient of any other velocity.
notes.TorusEuler.norm_stationaryShear_le: For every $x\in\mathbb R^3$ and every real $\rho$ with $|\rho|\le1$, the formal statement proves $|\sin(2\pi x_2)(e_1+\rho e_3)|\le2$ in the Euclidean vector norm. This is a pointwise bound for the stationary velocity $U_0$ and hence a uniform bound on the torus $\mathbb R^3/\mathbb Z^3$. It needs no frequency threshold or time interval. The permitted tilt range includes zero and negative values, whereas the construction uses $0<\rho\le1$. The sharper exact maximum is not stated by this declaration.
notes.TorusEuler.norm_sub_liftConvolution_scal: Let $f:\mathbb R^3\to E$ be a bounded $C^k$ function into a complex Banach space, with $k\ge1$. Let $\psi$ be smooth, equal to one on the unit ball and zero outside the radius-two ball, and let $\Lambda>0$. If $\|D^kf(z+v)-D^kf(z)\|\le A_v$ for all $z$, then the formal statement bounds the increment at translation $v$ of $f-K_\Lambda*f$ by $\Lambda^{-k}A_v\int|y|^k|\check\psi(y)|\,dy$. Here $D^kf$ uses the operator norm. Choosing $A_v$ proportional to $|v|^{1/2}$ supplies the Hölder part of the tail estimate. This result estimates one translated increment, not the full $C^{s,1/2}$ norm in (B.2).

Let $f:\mathbb R^3\to E$ be a bounded $C^k$ function into a complex Banach space, $k\ge1$, with $\|D^kf(z)\|\le A$ everywhere. Let $\psi$ be smooth, equal to one on the unit ball and zero outside the radius-two ball, and let $\Lambda>0$. The formal statement proves $|f(x)-K_\Lambda*f(x)|\le\Lambda^{-k}A\int|y|^k|\check\psi(y)|\,dy$ for all $x$. The norm on the derivative tensor is its operator norm. Unit mass and the vanishing moments remove the Taylor polynomial. Periodicity is unnecessary. The result supplies the uniform part of (B.2); spatial derivative and increment estimates are separate steps.
notes.TorusEuler.norm_wavePotential_le: Let $\kappa\in\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\}$, and let $V$ be a continuous period-one phase profile with $\int_0^1V=0$. Suppose $|V(s)|\le B$ for $0\le s\le1$. The formal statement proves $|Q[V](s)|\le2B/|\kappa|$ for every real $s$, where $Q[V]=-\partial_s^{-1}(\kappa\times V/|\kappa|^2)$ and the primitive has zero phase mean. All norms here are Euclidean. Transversality is not needed for this estimate. This supplies the inverse-frequency factor described after (3.6); forming $C[V]=\mathbf d\times Q[V]$ still requires one label derivative and its coefficient bounds.
notes.TorusEuler.norm_wavePrimaryPressure_geom: Let $N\ge1$, $B,D\ge0$, vectors $\kappa,g_c$ and operators $H_\phi,H_c$ satisfy $|\kappa|,\|H_\phi\|\le DN$, $|F||g_c|,|F||c|\le D\sqrt N B$ and $\|PH_c\|\le DB$. Then $\|-F(g_c\otimes\kappa+\kappa\otimes g_c+cH_\phi)-PH_c\|\le(3D^2+D)N\sqrt N B$. In (5.51), these symbols represent the terms left after removing $-c_{\mathbf a}F_h\,{}^{\prime}\kappa\otimes\kappa$, with $g_c=\nabla c_{\mathbf a}$ and $H_\phi=D^2\phi$. This is a pointwise tensor estimate in operator norm. Obtaining the paper’s $\lambda^{-3/4}$ decay additionally uses $N=\lambda$ and the pressure profile bound $B=O(\mathsf D^C\lambda^{-9/4})$.
notes.TorusEuler.norm_waveProfile_le: For the selected bump-based family, every $0<h\le1$ and every real phase satisfy $|F_h(s)|\le h/2$. This is a pointwise statement, hence also a supremum bound over the unit phase period. It sharpens the constant in the $O(h)$ amplitude conclusion of Lemma 3.1. In an affine wave, multiplication by $|\mathbf a|$ gives velocity amplitude at most $h|\mathbf a|/2$. The profile can nevertheless have unit slope at zero, so the estimate does not make the central velocity gradient small. The formal conclusion is the width bound, not the intermediate bound $2c_h$ in terms of bump mass.
notes.TorusEuler.normalizeDerivOfScaled: Let $v$ be a path in a real inner-product space, nonzero at the evaluated time, with derivative $v'=|v|w$ relative to a time set. Put $\widehat v=v/|v|$. The formal statement proves $\widehat v'=w-(\widehat v\cdot w)\widehat v$. Taking $w=v'/|v|$ gives $(\operatorname{Id}-\widehat v\widehat v^T)v'/|v|$, the normalization formula in the proof of Lemma 2.2. The conclusion is local in time and does not assume a wave equation. Nonvanishing is essential: normalization is defined as zero at a zero vector, but no derivative formula there is claimed.
notes.TorusEuler.odd_transportedProfile: Fix a time and suppose $A(t,-x)=-A(t,x)$. Let the profile satisfy $f(t,-a,-s)=-f(t,a,s)$ for every label and phase. The formal statement proves that $x\mapsto f(t,A(t,x),k_*\cdot A(t,x))$ is odd for any $k_*\in\mathbb R^3$. This is the final evaluation step in the parity argument of §3.1. It is purely algebraic and requires no derivatives, periodicity or nonzero covector. The result applies to the directly evaluated profile; the separate extension from the centered label cell must preserve the same reflection symmetry to obtain the full periodic wave.
notes.TorusEuler.odd_waveProfile: For $0<h\le1$, the formal statement gives $F_h(-s)=-F_h(s)$ for every real phase. Here $F_h(s)=\int_0^s S_h(r)\,dr$, with $S_h$ the normalized periodized bump slope, which is even. Thus the chosen normalization $F_h(0)=0$ fixes the odd primitive. This proves the parity required in Lemma 3.1. The theorem does not, by itself, state periodicity or the existence of the pressure primitive; those use the zero phase mean and further integral identities. No assertion about arbitrary widths or arbitrary odd wave families is made.
notes.TorusEuler.oscillatoryPhasePressure_prim: For a fixed matrix $M$, vectors $\kappa,\mathbf a$, scalar cutoff $\theta$, and profile width $h$, the phase pressure selected for the zero-source wave $\theta\mathbf aF_h$ is $-c_{\mathbf a}P_h$, where $c_{\mathbf a}=2\theta(\kappa\cdot M\mathbf a)/|\kappa|^2$ and $P_h$ is the zero-mean periodic primitive of $F_h$. With $\theta=\widetilde\chi g$, this is the leading pressure in Lemma 5.9. The identity is algebraic and does not require positivity of the coupling or transversality. It also holds at $\kappa=0$ under the convention that division by zero is zero; the paper’s transported carrier is nonzero.
notes.TorusEuler.oscillatoryPhasePressure_weig: The time index is arbitrary and the multiplier $g^{-1}$ is not differentiated. If $g=0$, the formal inverse is zero; the fluid application takes a positive weight. The zero-mean primitive in (5.16) gives bounds for $\lambda\mathsf p$ in terms of the weighted velocity and source derivatives. Smoothness, phase periodicity and zero phase means are assumed, along with bounds for the normalized coefficients. Summing these derivative estimates and inserting the parent bounds yields (5.24), with no extra power of the frequency lost to pressure recovery.
notes.TorusEuler.oscillatoryTransverseProjecti: For a vector $\kappa$ in the real inner-product space, the formal operator is $v\mapsto v-\kappa(\kappa\cdot v)/|\kappa|^2$. When $\kappa\ne0$, this is the orthogonal projection onto $\kappa^\perp$, written $I-P_\kappa$ in (5.4). At $\kappa=0$, the reciprocal of $|\kappa|^2$ is defined as zero, so the operator is the identity; the formula is therefore defined for every vector. In the paper, nonvanishing follows from $k_*\ne0$ and invertibility of the parent flow. Applying this projection does not by itself prove that the projected initial seed is nonzero at nearby labels.
notes.TorusEuler.oscillatory_transverse_of_ini: Let $J$ be a time interval containing $t_0$. Assume $\kappa$ never vanishes on $J$ and satisfies $\kappa_t=-M^T\kappa$. Suppose the amplitude satisfies $V_t=-MV+2\kappa(\kappa\cdot MV)/|\kappa|^2+f-\kappa(\kappa\cdot f)/|\kappa|^2$. If $\kappa(t_0)\cdot V(t_0)=0$, the formal statement proves $\kappa(t)\cdot V(t)=0$ for every $t\in J$. The projected forcing cancels in the derivative of the pairing. Setting $f=0$ gives the persistence asserted after (3.2). The theorem assumes the paths and their differential equations; it does not construct them or establish smooth dependence on particle labels.
notes.TorusEuler.paperA1_displacement_eq_primi: Let $z,v$ be curves of divergence-free half-Hölder fields on the unit torus. If $v$ is continuous on $[0,1]$, $z_t=v$ there with derivatives taken within the interval, and $z(0)=0$, then $z(t)=\int_0^tv(s)\,ds$ for every $t\in[0,1]$. This is the fundamental theorem of calculus used in Theorem A.1. No terminal condition is needed for this identity; $z(1)=0$ is equivalent to the additional zero-time-mean condition on $v$.
notes.TorusEuler.paperA1_solution_of_unproject: On $[0,1]$, let $z_t=v$, with continuous divergence-free half-Hölder velocity, zero displacement at both endpoints, and constant divergence-free $c$. Suppose $Kv-J(\Omega v)+L=c+G$ and $G$ is the gradient of a periodic differentiable potential at every time. Then the same $v,c$ form a projected endpoint solution, and $z=Jv$. This is the passage from an arbitrary solution of Theorem A.1 to the class where the inverse gives uniqueness. It proves that passage, not existence or uniqueness of the projected solution itself. Here $Jw(t)=\int_0^tw(s)\,ds$.
notes.TorusEuler.paperA2_wordNorm_le: Fix an integer $N\ge0$ and nonnegative bounds $a,p,b,F$. Suppose every coefficient derivative through order $N$ has size between zero and $b$, every source derivative has size at most $F$, and each solution derivative is bounded by $a$ times its source plus $p$ times the Leibniz correction terms. Each correction uses a nonempty set of derivatives on the coefficient and therefore a lower-order solution derivative. Then every solution derivative through order $N$ is at most $\max(1,a(1+p2^N(2b)))^{N+1}F$. This is a numerical induction; identifying the sequences with genuine derivatives is a separate hypothesis in its application to Lemma A.2.
notes.TorusEuler.paperAppendixD_holderComparis: Each coordinate multi-index is counted once; the half-Hölder summand uses the maximum of the supremum and difference-quotient bounds. For $0<\ell_*\le1$, the finite supremum norm is bounded by the half-Hölder norm, which is at most $4\ell_*^{-1/2}$ times the supremum norm one order higher. Smoothness and finiteness of the derivative bounds are explicit. This is the comparison (D.2) responsible for the single source-derivative loss in Proposition 5.2.
notes.TorusEuler.paperHierarchyActiveVelocityN: Each multi-index occurs once. The definition assigns zero when dividing by a zero weight, but the active-interval estimates assume $\gamma>0$ and finite derivative bounds. This measures a field on $[t_0,T]$ in the scaled label and phase norm, divided by the positive amplitude weight $\gamma(t)$. Time indexes the supremum and is not differentiated. It is used in the version of (5.20) for data defined only after activation, without requiring fields at earlier times.
notes.TorusEuler.paperLemma13_slowOrders: Let $b\ge1$ be an integer, $K(s)=320b(s+1)$, and $\mathcal B(s)>0$ satisfy $\log\mathcal B(s)\ge4K(s+1)^3$ for $s\ge1$. Suppose $\lambda_0\ge\mathcal B(1)$, $q_1=1$, $\lambda_j=\lambda_{j-1}^{K(q_j)}$, and $q_{j+1}=\max\{1\le s\le q_j+1:\mathcal B(s)\le\lambda_{j-1}\}$. Then $q_j\le q_{j+1}\le q_j+1$, $q_j\to\infty$, and $4\log\lambda_{j+2}\le(\log\lambda_{j-1})^2$ for $j\ge1$. Thus the last expression is exactly (1.15), since $L_{j+1}=4\log\lambda_{j+2}$. The formal statement omits threshold monotonicity and analytic-cost domination from §1.5; the arithmetic result therefore applies under fewer assumptions.
notes.TorusEuler.paperLemma31_waveProfile: The theorem supplies smooth one-periodic profiles $F_h,P_h$ for $0<h\le1$, with $F_h$ odd, $P_h'=F_h$, and $P_h$ of mean zero. One constant $C>0$, independent of $h$ and phase $s$, satisfies $F_h'(0)=1$, $-Ch\le F_h'(s)\le1$ and $|F_h(s)|\le Ch$. For each integer $j\ge2$, a constant $C_j>0$ is chosen before $h,s$ and gives $|F_h^{(j)}(s)|\le C_jh^{1-j}$. The exponent $1-j$ is an integer and may be negative; it is not truncated to zero. These are the existence and uniformity assertions of Lemma 3.1. No regularity in the parameter $h$ is asserted.
notes.TorusEuler.paperLemma57_periodicGraphFro: At a fixed time, let $A$ be a smooth invertible label map commuting with integer translations. Let $f(a,s)$ be smooth and agree with a smooth periodic mean whenever some $|a_i|>1/2-\delta$, where $0<\delta\le1/2$. The field obtained by evaluating $f$ on $s=k_*\cdot a$ in the centered cell and repeating it periodically is smooth and periodic. With $\ell_*,h>0$, $h=\lambda^{-1/2}$, $|k_*|\le\mathsf D\lambda$, $\ell_*^{-1}\le\mathsf D^a$, inverse-coefficient bounds through order $m+1$, and corresponding scaled derivative bounds for $f$, it also satisfies the derivative and $C^{m,1/2}$ estimates of Lemma 5.7. The collar assumption explicitly supplies the continuation across cell faces. This theorem is spatial at one time; it does not assert joint smoothness in time.
notes.TorusEuler.paperLemma61_exists_firstWave: Assume $0<\rho\le1$, $T\ge0$, $\lambda>0$ and $T\|B_\rho\|\le1/8$, where $B_\rho=2\pi(e_1+\rho e_3)\otimes e_2$. The formal theorem gives a first central wave with $\kappa(0)=\lambda e_1$, positive initial amplitude along $e_2$, nonzero transversality and attained peak $\lambda^{-3/4}$. It satisfies $\lambda^{1/4}/2\le|\kappa(0)||\mathbf a(0)|\le\lambda^{1/4}$ and, for every $\mathsf D\ge2$, $\nu\ge\mathsf D^{-1}$ and $|\mathbf b(t)|/\gamma(t)\le\mathsf D|\mathbf b(t')|/\gamma(t')$ for transverse solutions and $0\le t'\le t\le T$, with $\gamma=\lambda^{3/4}|\mathbf a|$. Unlike the numbered formal statement of Lemma 6.1, this version allows $T=0$ and every positive frequency, including frequencies below one.
notes.TorusEuler.paperLemma61_firstWave: Let $\kappa,\mathbf a$ be any first central wave over $B_\rho=2\pi(e_1+\rho e_3)\otimes e_2$, with initial covector $\lambda e_1$, positive initial amplitude along $e_2$, nonzero transversality and attained peak $\lambda^{-3/4}$ on $[0,T]$. If $0<\rho\le1$, $\lambda>0$ and $T\|B_\rho\|\le1/8$, its initial strength lies in $[\lambda^{1/4}/2,\lambda^{1/4}]$. For every $\mathsf D\ge2$ it satisfies $\nu(t)\ge\mathsf D^{-1}$ and $|\mathbf b(t)|/\gamma(t)\le\mathsf D|\mathbf b(t')|/\gamma(t')$ for transverse amplitude solutions and ordered times, where $\gamma=\lambda^{3/4}|\mathbf a|$. This statement assumes the wave has already been given and proves the estimates for every such choice. It does not require $\lambda\ge1$.
notes.TorusEuler.paperLemmaA2_mixed_holder: Let $H=L^2([0,1];\mathbb R^3)$ and $\mathcal R=\mathbb P\mathcal Q$, with $\mathcal Q$ subtracting the time average. Suppose $B\in C^{1,1/2}(\mathbb T^3;\mathcal L(H))$ and $\langle B(a)w,w\rangle\ge\mu\|w\|^2$ for zero-mean paths, with $\mu>0$. Then $\mathcal RB$ is invertible on $\mathcal RC^{0,1/2}$ and $\|v\|\le C(2+\mu^{-1}+\|B\|_\infty+\|D_aB\|_\infty)^{145}\|\mathcal RBv\|$. This is only the time-path case of Lemma A.2. The constant is independent of the coefficient and datum; higher regularity and the spatial-vector case are separate results.
notes.TorusEuler.paperLemmaA2_mixed_holder_bou: Let $H=L^2([0,1];\mathbb R^3)$, $\mathcal R=\mathbb P\mathcal Q$, and $B\in C^{n,1/2}(\mathbb T^3;\mathcal L(H))$ for an integer $n\ge0$. Then $v\mapsto\mathcal R(Bv)$ maps projected $C^{n,1/2}$ fields to the same class, with norm at most $C$ times the input norm. The constant may depend on $B$ and $n$, but is chosen before $v$. Time remains an $L^2$ variable. This is the forward bound in Lemma A.2 and needs no coercivity assumption or inverse theorem.

Let $H=L^2([0,1];\mathbb R^3)$ and $\mathcal R=\mathbb P\mathcal Q$. Suppose $B\in C^{k,1/2}(\mathbb T^3;\mathcal L(H))$ for an integer $k\ge1$, and $\langle B(a)w,w\rangle\ge\mu\|w\|^2$ on zero-time-mean paths with $\mu>0$. There is a base half-Hölder inverse of $\mathcal RB$ that maps every projected $C^{k,1/2}$ datum to a solution in that class with bound $\|v\|_{C^{k,1/2}}\le C\|f\|_{C^{k,1/2}}$. The constant may depend on $B,k,\mu$, not on $f$. The formal order is written $k=n+1$, covering precisely the positive integer orders.
notes.TorusEuler.paperLemmaA2_mixed_holder_res: With $H=L^2([0,1];\mathbb R^3)$ and $\mathcal R=\mathbb P\mathcal Q$, assume $B\in C^{k,1/2}$, integer $k\ge1$, and positive coercivity on zero-time-mean paths at each label. Then $\mathcal R(Bv)$ belongs to $C^{k,1/2}$ whenever projected $v$ does, and every projected datum $f$ in that class has a unique projected solution $v$ of $\mathcal R(Bv)=f$ in the same class. This is the higher existence and uniqueness assertion of Lemma A.2 for time paths. The statement does not include a numerical norm bound; that bound is proved separately.
notes.TorusEuler.paperLemmaA2_spatial_holder: Suppose $B\in C^{1,1/2}(\mathbb T^3;\mathcal L(\mathbb R^3))$ and $B(a)w\cdot w\ge\mu|w|^2$ for every label and vector, with $\mu>0$. Then $v\mapsto\mathbb P(Bv)$ is invertible on divergence-free $C^{0,1/2}$ fields, with $\|v\|\le C(2+\mu^{-1}+\|B\|_\infty+\|D_aB\|_\infty)^{145}\|\mathbb P(Bv)\|$. The constant is chosen before $B,\mu$ and the datum. This proves the spatial-vector case of Lemma A.2 and fixes a polynomial exponent where the paper leaves it unspecified. The time-path case and higher norms are separate statements.
notes.TorusEuler.paperLemmaA2_spatial_holder_b: For an integer $n\ge0$, suppose the matrix coefficient $B$ belongs to $C^{n,1/2}(\mathbb T^3)$. If $v$ is divergence free and in the same class, then $\mathbb P(Bv)$ belongs to $C^{n,1/2}$ and $\|\mathbb P(Bv)\|_{C^{n,1/2}}\le C\|v\|_{C^{n,1/2}}$. The constant may depend on $B,n$, but is uniform in $v$. This is the forward-map bound used in the final assertion of Lemma A.2. Coercivity is unnecessary for multiplication and projection; it is needed only for the inverse direction.

Let $B\in C^{k,1/2}(\mathbb T^3;\mathcal L(\mathbb R^3))$, where $k\ge1$ is an integer, and assume $B(a)w\cdot w\ge\mu|w|^2$ for all $a,w$, with $\mu>0$. The base half-Hölder inverse of $\mathbb PB$ maps every divergence-free $C^{k,1/2}$ datum to a solution in the same class, with $\|v\|_{C^{k,1/2}}\le C\|f\|_{C^{k,1/2}}$. The constant is uniform in $f$ but may depend on $B,k,\mu$. The formal positive order is written as $n+1$. No single polynomial estimate uniform over all higher orders is asserted.
notes.TorusEuler.paperLemmaA2_spatial_holder_r: For an integer $k\ge1$, let $B\in C^{k,1/2}(\mathbb T^3;\mathcal L(\mathbb R^3))$ satisfy the positive pointwise quadratic lower bound with constant $\mu>0$. Then $v\mapsto\mathbb P(Bv)$ preserves divergence-free $C^{k,1/2}$ fields, and every divergence-free datum of that regularity has a unique preimage in the same class. This is the higher regularity solvability assertion of Lemma A.2 for spatial vectors. The formal order $n+1$ ranges over all positive integers; quantitative higher norm bounds are supplied by separate results.
notes.TorusEuler.paperLemmaB1_bernstein: Let $\psi$ be smooth, zero outside the radius-two ball and one on the unit ball. For each integer $m\ge0$, the formal statement supplies $C_m\ge0$ such that, for $\Lambda\ge1$ and a continuous complex Banach-valued torus field with no frequencies above $4\Lambda$, the sum of the supremum norms of all ordered $m$-fold coordinate derivatives is at most $C_m\Lambda^m\|f\|_\infty$. Spatial derivatives are taken on the periodic lift to $\mathbb R^3$. Mixed partials occur repeatedly in this sum, whereas (B.1) counts each multi-index once. The estimate therefore implies the multi-index bound for this target class, but it does not state the paper's arbitrary real normed-space version.
notes.TorusEuler.paperLemmaB1_bernstein_real_m: Fix a smooth symbol equal to one on the unit ball and zero outside the radius-two ball. For every integer $m\ge0$, the formal statement chooses $C_m$ before the real normed target space, the frequency $\Lambda\ge1$, and the continuous torus field $f$. If every scalar measurement of $f$ has Fourier coefficients zero above $4\Lambda$, it proves $\sum_{|\beta|=m}\|\partial^\beta f\|_\infty\le C_m\Lambda^m\|f\|_\infty$. Derivatives use the periodic lift to $\mathbb R^3$, and increasing coordinate sequences count each multi-index once. No completeness assumption on the real target is needed. This is the scope and counting convention of (B.1).
notes.TorusEuler.paperLemmaB1_cutoff_LInfinity: Let $g$ be a measurable essentially bounded field on $\mathbb T^3=\mathbb R^3/\mathbb Z^3$ with values in a complex normed space. For a smooth symbol $\psi$ vanishing outside the radius-two ball and $\Lambda>0$, the formal statement gives $\|S_\Lambda g\|_{L^\infty}\le\|\check\psi\|_{L^1(\mathbb R^3)}\|g\|_{L^\infty}$. The measure has total mass one and these are essential suprema. No completeness hypothesis appears in this declaration; for an incomplete target, the integration convention used by the formalization assigns zero rather than a general Banach-valued integral. For a Banach target the usual Fourier-integral interpretation applies. The numbered Lemma B.1 restricts its complex branch to that complete setting. This result does not include a Hölder estimate.
notes.TorusEuler.paperLemmaB1_cutoff_aeBound: Let $g$ be an integrable complex normed-space-valued field on the unit-volume three-dimensional torus, with $|g|\le M$ almost everywhere and $M\ge0$. For a smooth symbol supported in the radius-two ball and $\Lambda>0$, the formal statement proves $|S_\Lambda g(x)|\le M\|\check\psi\|_{L^1}$ at every point. The output is a finite Fourier sum, so its bound is pointwise. Completeness of the target is not assumed; if the target is incomplete, the formal integral convention assigns zero and the formula need not describe ordinary Fourier integration in that space. The paper's finite-dimensional targets avoid this issue. This is the value estimate behind the $L^\infty$ bound, with no spatial-increment conclusion.
notes.TorusEuler.paperLemmaB1_cutoff_commutes_: Let $g$ be a continuous complex Banach-valued field on $\mathbb T^3$, whose periodic lift $f$ to $\mathbb R^3$ is $C^m$. Assume $\psi$ is smooth and zero outside the radius-two ball, and $\Lambda>0$. The formal statement proves $D^m(S_\Lambda f)=K_\Lambda*D^mf$, with $K_\Lambda(y)=\Lambda^3\check\psi(\Lambda y)$. Both sides are multilinear derivative tensors. Periodicity and continuity bound the derivatives on all of $\mathbb R^3$. To write the right side as $S_\Lambda(D^mf)$, one also uses the convolution representation for that tensor field. The result supplies spatial commutation only; time differentiation is treated separately.
notes.TorusEuler.paperLemmaB1_cutoff_derivativ: Let $g$ be a continuous complex Banach-valued torus field whose periodic lift $f$ belongs to $C^{m,1/2}$. For $\Lambda>0$ and a smooth symbol supported in the radius-two ball, the formal statement gives $D^m(S_\Lambda f)=K_\Lambda*D^mf$, where $K_\Lambda(y)=\Lambda^3\check\psi(\Lambda y)$. The Hölder hypothesis includes differentiability and bounded derivatives through order $m$. The conclusion is an identity of derivative tensors on $\mathbb R^3$ and supplies a spatial commutation step in Appendix B. It neither differentiates in time nor proves the entire tail estimate; a separate result gives the same identity under the weaker $C^m$ assumption. The underlying higher-order Hölder definition is not included in this packet; the norm interpretation follows its supplied description.
notes.TorusEuler.paperLemmaB1_cutoff_holder: Let $f$ be the periodic lift of a continuous complex Banach-valued torus field and assume $f\in C^{0,1/2}$. If $\psi$ is smooth and zero outside the radius-two ball and $\Lambda>0$, the formal statement proves $S_\Lambda f\in C^{0,1/2}$ and $\|S_\Lambda f\|_{C^{0,1/2}}\le\|\check\psi\|_{L^1}\|f\|_{C^{0,1/2}}$. Here the Hölder norm is the sum of the uniform norm and half-Hölder seminorm of the periodic lift. The constant does not depend on $\Lambda$ or $f$. No plateau or evenness assumption is needed. This is the Hölder bound in Lemma B.1, not its separate measurable-input essential-supremum estimate.
notes.TorusEuler.paperLemmaB1_cutoff_sup: Let $g$ be continuous on $\mathbb T^3=\mathbb R^3/\mathbb Z^3$ with values in a complex Banach space. For $\Lambda>0$ and a smooth real symbol $\psi$ zero outside the radius-two ball, the formal statement gives $\sup_x|S_\Lambda g(x)|\le\|\check\psi\|_{L^1(\mathbb R^3)}\sup_x|g(x)|$. The supremum on the output may be taken over its periodic lift. Compactness guarantees boundedness of the input, while rapid decay makes the kernel integral finite. This proves the continuous-input uniform bound in Appendix B; it is not itself a claim about all measurable $L^\infty$ inputs or the half-Hölder norm.
notes.TorusEuler.paperLemmaB1_cutoff_support_p: Let $g$ be a continuous complex Banach-valued torus field and let the real symbol $\psi$ be even. The formal statement proves that the finite cutoff has no Fourier modes outside $|\xi|\le2\Lambda$ and preserves any relation $g(-x)=c\,g(x)$ with real $c$. Taking $c=-1$ gives oddness and $c=1$ gives evenness. These conclusions follow from the symmetric finite frequency set and the even symbol; smoothness, a plateau and positivity of $\Lambda$ are unnecessary for this algebraic statement. It supplies two parts of Lemma B.1, but it contains no assertion about divergence.
notes.TorusEuler.paperLemmaB1_cutoff_tail: Let $\psi$ be smooth, zero outside the radius-two ball and equal to one on the unit ball. For each integer $M\ge0$, the formal statement supplies $C_M\ge0$ such that, for $\Lambda\ge1$, $0\le s\le M$, and a continuous complex Banach-valued torus field with periodic lift $f\in C^{M,1/2}$, the remainder belongs to $C^{s,1/2}$ and satisfies $\|(I-S_\Lambda)f\|_{C^{s,1/2}}\le C_M\Lambda^{s-M}\|f\|_{C^{M,1/2}}$. The exponent $s-M$ is an integer difference, so negative exponents mean reciprocal powers. These norms sum uniform and Hölder bounds for derivative tensors through the indicated order. The constant is uniform in $s$, frequency and field. This result concerns the complex cutoff; the real-velocity estimate is separate. The underlying higher-order Hölder definition is not included in this packet; the norm interpretation follows its supplied description.
notes.TorusEuler.paperLemmaB1_realBanachCutoff: Let $g$ be a measurable essentially bounded field on the unit-volume three-dimensional torus with values in a real Banach space. For $\Lambda>0$ and a smooth symbol $\psi$ supported in the radius-two ball, the formal statement proves $\|S_\Lambda g\|_{L^\infty}\le\|\check\psi\|_{L^1}\|g\|_{L^\infty}$. The real cutoff is formed using a complexification of the target and then taking its real component. The norms here are essential suprema; no continuity assumption is made. The same frequency-independent constant as in the complex estimate applies. This extends the real-velocity $L^\infty$ bound but contains no Hölder conclusion.
notes.TorusEuler.paperLemmaB1_realCutoff_LInfi: Let $g:\mathbb T^3\to\mathbb R^3$ be measurable and essentially bounded for the torus measure of total mass one. If $\psi$ is smooth and zero outside the radius-two ball and $\Lambda>0$, the formal statement proves $\|S_\Lambda g\|_{L^\infty}\le\|\check\psi\|_{L^1(\mathbb R^3)}\|g\|_{L^\infty}$. The cutoff is defined by complex Fourier coefficients followed by the real part, and its output is a finite Fourier sum. This supplies the measurable real-input estimate mentioned in Lemma B.1. It is broader in input regularity than the continuous real-velocity supremum clause inside the numbered formal statement.
notes.TorusEuler.paperLemmaB1_realCutoff_admis: Let $g$ be a continuous real velocity on $\mathbb T^3$ with smooth periodic lift to $\mathbb R^3$, and let $\psi$ be even. The formal statement says that the real cutoff preserves oddness and divergence freeness whenever the input has those properties, and that every output Fourier coefficient outside $|\xi|\le2\Lambda$ vanishes. These are conditional conclusions, not assumptions that every input is odd or incompressible. No radiality, smoothness of the symbol or positive-scale hypothesis is required for this finite-sum identity. It supplies the velocity properties needed in Subsection 5.7, but evenness preservation is stated in the separate parity result.
notes.TorusEuler.paperLemmaB1_realCutoff_parit: Suppose $g:\mathbb T^3\to\mathbb R^3$ is continuous and satisfies $g(-x)=c\,g(x)$ for a real constant $c$, and suppose $\psi$ is even. The formal statement proves the same reflection identity for the real cutoff $S_\Lambda g$. In particular, it preserves oddness when $c=-1$ and evenness when $c=1$. The result concerns a finite Fourier sum and holds for every real scale, without a smoothness or support condition on the symbol. The paper uses the positive-scale cutoff with its prescribed smooth symbol. This declaration proves parity only, not divergence preservation or operator estimates.
notes.TorusEuler.paperLemmaB1_realCutoff_sup: Let $g:\mathbb T^3\to\mathbb R^3$ be continuous, let $\psi$ be smooth and zero outside the radius-two ball, and let $\Lambda>0$. The formal statement gives $\sup_x|S_\Lambda g(x)|\le\|\check\psi\|_{L^1(\mathbb R^3)}\sup_x|g(x)|$, with the output evaluated on its periodic lift. The real cutoff is the real part of the corresponding complex Fourier sum. The bound is uniform in $\Lambda$ and $g$, and requires neither a plateau nor evenness. It is a continuous-input supremum bound; the essential-supremum estimate for measurable real velocities is a distinct result.
notes.TorusEuler.paperLemmaD1_derivatives: Let $f(t,a,s)$ be smooth in label and phase, let $\ell_*,h>0$, and assume all weighted mixed derivatives through order $n+1$ are bounded uniformly in time, label and phase. The formal statement proves $\sum_{i=1}^3\|\partial_{a_i}f\|_{[n]}\le3\ell_*^{-1}\|f\|_{[n+1]}$ and $\|\partial_sf\|_{[n]}\le h^{-1}\|f\|_{[n+1]}$. Each multi-index is counted once in the finite norms. Applying the inequalities to $f/\gamma(t)$ gives (D.3), because the weight depends only on time. This declaration itself is unweighted and does not assume periodicity or positivity of an amplitude function.
notes.TorusEuler.paperLemmaD1_phaseAverage: Let $f(t,a,s)$ take values in a real Banach space and be smooth in $(a,s)$, one-periodic in $s$, and have bounded derivatives through order $n$ along a fixed finite ordered family of constant directions. The formal statement proves $\|\langle f\rangle_s\|_{[n]}\le\|f\|_{[n]}$ and $\|f-\langle f\rangle_s\|_{[n]}\le2\|f\|_{[n]}$, where the derivative sum uses that specified family. Choosing the scaled label and phase directions gives the norms of Appendix D, and applying the result to $f/\gamma(t)$ gives their weighted form. The time set is arbitrary and all suprema include it. The normalized primitive estimate in (D.5) is not part of this declaration.
notes.TorusEuler.paperLemmaD1_phasePrimitive: Let $f(t,a,s)$ take values in a real Banach space and be smooth, one-periodic in $s$, have zero phase average at every $(t,a)$, and have bounded derivatives through order $n$ along a fixed finite family of constant directions. The formal statement proves that its normalized phase primitive has finite derivative expression at most twice that of $f$. With directions $\ell_*\partial_{a_i}$ and $h\partial_s$, this is the primitive estimate of (D.5); applying it to $f/\gamma(t)$ yields the positive-amplitude weighted version. The supremum includes the whole chosen time set. This declaration is the derivative-norm estimate, whereas periodicity and recovery of the input by phase differentiation are established separately.
notes.TorusEuler.paperLemmaD1_product: For smooth fields $f,g$, a continuous bilinear map $B$, and smooth prescribed differentiation directions, assume their finite derivative families are bounded, with the second field measured after division by $\gamma(t)$. The formal statement bounds the finite norm of $B(f,g)/\gamma$ by $2^{n+1}N_n\|B\|$ times the product of those two finite norms, where $N_n$ counts the increasing derivative sequences of length at most $n$. It applies to supremum norms and to the maximum convention for half-Hölder norms. Unlike the paper's amplitude weight, $\gamma$ need not be positive here: division by zero gives the zero field at that time. For $\gamma>0$ and the scaled coordinate directions, it yields (D.4).
notes.TorusEuler.paperLemmaD2_inverse: Let $\mathsf D\ge1$ and let $q$ be a nonnegative integer. Suppose $c(t,a)$ is smooth in the label, $\|D_a^mc(t,a)\|\le C_m\mathsf D^{q(m+1)}$ uniformly in time and label for every $m$, and every $c(t,a)$ is invertible in a complete real normed algebra. If $\|c(t,a)^{-1}\|\le\mathsf D^q$, the formal statement gives analogous derivative-tensor bounds for $c^{-1}$ with exponent $3q$. Invertibility is required at every point, so the inverse is the usual algebra inverse throughout the domain. The constants are obtained for the fixed coefficient and parent parameter; their uniform selection over varying inputs is stated separately in the full Lemma D.2.
notes.TorusEuler.paperLemmaD2_inverse_multiInd: Let $\mathsf D\ge1$, let $q$ be a nonnegative integer, and let $c:I\times\mathbb R^3\to A$ be smooth with values in a complete real normed algebra. Assume $|c|_m\le C_m\mathsf D^{q(m+1)}$ for every $m$, with bounded coordinate derivatives, pointwise invertibility, and $\|c^{-1}\|_\infty\le\mathsf D^q$. The formal statement gives $|c^{-1}|_m\le C'_m\mathsf D^{3q(m+1)}$, counting each multi-index once. Supremum bounds include every time in $I$. The constants are asserted for the fixed coefficient and parent parameter, not uniformly across families. The numbered Lemma D.2 supplies that stronger quantifier order.
notes.TorusEuler.paperLemmaD2_mul: Let $\mathsf D\ge1$ and $q\ge0$ be an integer. Suppose two coefficients $c,d:I\times\mathbb R^3\to A$ are smooth and their spatial derivative tensors have uniform bounds $\|D^mc\|\le C_m\mathsf D^{q(m+1)}$ and $\|D^md\|\le C'_m\mathsf D^{q(m+1)}$, with $A$ a real normed algebra. The formal statement proves the same form of estimate for $cd$ with exponent $2q$. It measures the operator norms of derivative tensors, not directly the coordinate sums $|c|_m$. An equivalence theorem converts between these measurements. Constants are asserted for the fixed inputs; the full Lemma D.2 separately states uniformity before choosing the parent parameter and fields.
notes.TorusEuler.paperLemmaD2_mul_multiIndex: Let $\mathsf D\ge1$ and let $q$ be a nonnegative integer. For smooth phase-independent coefficients $c,d:I\times\mathbb R^3\to A$ in a real normed algebra, assume bounded derivatives of every order and estimates $|c|_m\le C_m\mathsf D^{q(m+1)}$, $|d|_m\le C'_m\mathsf D^{q(m+1)}$. The formal statement gives $|cd|_m\le C''_m\mathsf D^{2q(m+1)}$ for all $m$, with each spatial multi-index counted once. All time and label values enter the suprema. This proves product closure for the fixed parent parameter and fields. It does not by itself assert constants uniform over those choices, or retain an arbitrary fixed real exponent without enlargement.
notes.TorusEuler.paperLemmaD2_weighted: Suppose $\mathsf D\ge1$, $q$ is a nonnegative integer, $\ell_*\ge0$, and $\ell_*\mathsf D^q\le1$. Let a smooth coefficient satisfy $\|D_a^mc\|\le C_m\mathsf D^{q(m+1)}$ uniformly in time and label. The formal statement bounds $\ell_*^m\|D_a^mc\|$ by $C_m\mathsf D^q$, and for $m\ge1$ by $C_m\mathsf D^{2q}\ell_*$. It also bounds the corresponding finite coordinate-derivative norm by an order-dependent constant times $\mathsf D^q$. Unlike the paper's positive radius and fixed real exponent, this result permits zero radius and only integer $q$. The constants are obtained after fixing the parent parameter and coefficient. Thus it supplies the algebraic gain in D.2(c) with those precise conventions.
notes.TorusEuler.paperLemmaD2_weighted_multiIn: Let $\mathsf D\ge1$, let $q$ be a nonnegative integer, and assume $0\le\ell_*$ and $\ell_*\mathsf D^q\le1$. If a smooth coefficient has bounded derivatives and $|c|_m\le C_m\mathsf D^{q(m+1)}$ for every $m$, the formal statement yields $\sum_{m\le n}\ell_*^m|c|_m\le(\sum_{m\le n}C_m)\mathsf D^q$ and $\ell_*^m|c|_m\le C_m\mathsf D^{2q}\ell_*$ for $m\ge1$. The derivative sums count each multi-index once and include the chosen time set. This is the coefficient-radius calculation of D.2(c), allowing zero radius and using integer exponents. Replacing the paper's fixed real exponent by its ceiling can require a strictly smaller radius.
notes.TorusEuler.paperLemmaD3_lifting: Let $L_0v+\sum_j B_j(c_j,v)=f$ in real vector spaces with seminorms and finitely many commuting derivatives; suppose the zero-order bound holds for every admissible $v$. For a linear equation with the stated commutation and product rules, coefficient bounds through order $n$ lift the uniform zero-order estimate to the finite derivative norm. The conclusion contains one factor $C_{\rm low}$; the remaining constant is determined by the order and coefficient bounds. This is the general estimate behind Lemma D.3, with constraints and prescribed data incorporated in the solution and forcing spaces.
notes.TorusEuler.paperMeanIntegratedMomentum: For coefficient curves $K,\Omega$, a source $L$, and a divergence-free half-Hölder velocity $v$, the expression is $K(t)v(t)-\int_0^t\Omega(s)v(s)\,ds+L(t)$ as a half-Hölder field on $\mathbb T^3$. Coefficients act pointwise in the spatial label. This is exactly the left side of (4.9), but does not assert that it equals a constant plus a gradient. It imposes neither $\int_0^Tv=0$ nor time regularity or integrability; those conditions belong to the solution and inverse theorems.
notes.TorusEuler.paperMean_inverse_scale: Let $D\ge1$ and let $L,C_K,C_\Omega,L_K,L_\Omega$ be nonnegative. Set $Q=D+L+C_K+C_\Omega+L_K+L_\Omega$. Then $Q\ge1$ and $4+D^2+2D^2(1+L)^2+C_K+C_\Omega+L_K+L_\Omega\le16Q^4$. In Theorem 4.2, $D$ bounds the inverse deformation, $L$ the transported gradient, and the remaining quantities bound coefficients and their first spatial derivatives. This elementary inequality combines reciprocal ellipticity and displacement coercivity into one polynomial scale. It does not establish any of those analytic bounds.
notes.TorusEuler.paperMean_projection_C1_gradi: Let $q$ be a continuously differentiable $\mathbb Z^3$-periodic scalar function on $\mathbb R^3$, and suppose its gradient represents a $C^{0,1/2}$ vector field $g$ on $\mathbb T^3$. Then $\mathbb Pg=0$. This is the pressure-removal step in Appendix A. A zero-mean normalization of $q$ is not needed. Periodicity is needed: a constant vector field is a gradient of a nonperiodic affine function, but the torus Leray projection preserves that constant field.
notes.TorusEuler.paperPhysicalStepExponent: For nonnegative integer exponents $a,r,a_{\rm mean}$, define $b=6r+5a+2a_{\rm mean}+160$. The terms correspond to the envelope scale, hierarchy loss and the coefficient cost in the mean-pressure estimate. This is one sufficient numerical exponent used for $C_{\rm step}=\Gamma_P\mathsf D^b$ in §5.6. The formula itself does not prove that any estimate is dominated; the subsequent inequalities verify that fact and choose $\Gamma_P$. It contains no dependence on derivative order, frequency or expansion depth. Depth dependence is allowed in the separate coefficient $\Gamma_P$.
notes.TorusEuler.paperProposition511_physicalC: Fix a smooth even Fourier multiplier equal to one on $|\xi|\le1$ and zero for $|\xi|>2$. For $P\ge2$, $T>0$ and $\Lambda\ge1$, take a smooth periodic odd divergence-free velocity $V$ with smooth residual $R_V$, its pressure, and an upper bound $sI$ for the pressure-Hessian change from the parent. The formal statement constructs the truncated child with odd divergence-free residual supported at frequencies at most $4\Lambda$. Writing $\epsilon=\Lambda^{2-P}(1+\|V\|_{C_tC^{P,1/2}})^2$ and $e=C\|R_V\|_{C_tC^{1,1/2}}+C_P\epsilon$, it bounds the $C_tC^{2,1/2}$ velocity change by $C_P\epsilon$, and the residual plus additional pressure Hessian by $e$. The inherited upper bound is $(s+e)I$. The exponent $2-P$ is integral and may be negative. The Hölder norms sum derivative supremum norms and half-Hölder seminorms through the specified order.
notes.TorusEuler.paperProposition51_parentCoef: Assume $0<T\le1$, $\mathsf D\ge1$, smooth periodic parent velocity and its flow, forward and inverse deformation bounds by $\mathsf D$, and positive-order velocity bounds $R_n\mathsf D^j$. The six families in Proposition 5.1 satisfy derivative bounds with common power $\mathsf D^{16m+16}$. The velocity derivative bounds, deformation bounds and activation normalization are supplied first. After weighting by a sufficiently small radius, the remaining power is independent of derivative order. This result isolates that coefficient conclusion from the separate composition estimate.
notes.TorusEuler.paperProposition51_parentComp: Assume $0<T\le1$, $\mathsf D\ge1$, smooth periodic parent velocity and flow, both deformation bounds and polynomial velocity derivative bounds. The target may be any real normed space. If $f$ has the derivative bounds assumed in Proposition 5.1, composition with the parent flow gives $\lVert D_a^m(f\circ X)\rVert\le C_m A_f\mathsf D^{6m}$. The constants depend on the prescribed derivative bounds, not on the chosen parent or field. This supplies (5.7) before the radius weights are inserted.
notes.TorusEuler.paperProposition51_weightedCo: Assume $\mathsf D\ge1$, $\ell_*,A_f,C_j\ge0$ and the pointwise derivative bound at all orders on $[0,T]$. Once the composed field has derivative growth $\mathsf D^{6m}$, the condition $\ell_*\mathsf D^6\le1$ bounds its finite weighted sum by $C_nA_f$. This is the second estimate in (5.8). The theorem performs the summation of an already established derivative bound; composition with the flow is handled by the preceding estimate.
notes.TorusEuler.paperTheorem71: The theorem chooses an integer $b\ge1$, a nondecreasing positive threshold $\mathcal B$ satisfying (1.13), and $N_1\ge\mathcal B(1)$. For every $N\ge N_1$, it constructs a scheduled sequence with initial frequency $N$ and strength constant $18e^3$. The velocities are smooth, odd and divergence free, with controlled residuals, localized oscillations, small spatial Hölder corrections, prescribed central crossings, and activation times accumulating at a finite positive time before every stage endpoint. This is an existence theorem for one selected threshold. The later paper statement of Theorem 7.1 quantifies over all thresholds above a chosen analytic majorant and records further identifications with the finite expansion; those assertions are not part of this shorter conclusion.
notes.TorusEuler.paperTheoremA1: On $[0,1]\times\mathbb T^3$, let $K,\Omega$ be time-continuous in $C^{0,1/2}$, spatially differentiable, with uniform value and first derivative bounds. Assume $K\ge\kappa I$ as quadratic forms, $\kappa>0$, and $\int(Kz_t\cdot z_t+\Omega z_t\cdot z)\ge\mu\int|z_t|^2$, $\mu>0$, for all $H^1_0$ paths. Every $L\in C_tC^{0,1/2}$ gives a unique velocity, zero endpoint displacement, constant solenoidal field and pressure gradient satisfying $Kv-J(\Omega v)+L=c+\nabla\phi$, where $Jv(t)=\int_0^tv$. The velocity bound is $CQ^{291}\|L\|_0$, with $Q=2+\kappa^{-1}+\mu^{-1}$ plus the four coefficient bounds. A zero-mean periodic potential is supplied; smooth data give smooth $z,c,\nabla\phi$. Unlike the numbered Theorem A.1, this result does not separately require symmetric $K$ or skew-symmetric $\Omega$.
notes.TorusEuler.paper_mean_columns: Assume $0<T\le1$, $\mathsf D\ge2$, a smooth periodic parent flow with both deformation and higher derivative bounds, and a coercive endpoint mean problem compatible with that flow. For every smooth mean solution of the endpoint problem and every sufficiently large fixed radius exponent $s$, the estimate has the form $\lVert B\rVert_{[n]}\le C_n\mathsf D^{b+2+2s}\lVert\bar f\rVert_{[n+1]}$. The constants and threshold are chosen before the parent. Fixing $s$ therefore gives Proposition 5.2's parent exponent independent of $n$.
notes.TorusEuler.paper_mean_hardy: In a complete real Hilbert space, let $0<T\le1$, $F_t=MF$, and let $M_t$ be continuous. Suppose $H^\#=-(M_t+M^2)\le I$ as quadratic forms. For any $v\in L^2([0,T])$ with zero integral, put $z=Jv$ and $\xi=Fz$. Then $\int H^\#\xi\cdot\xi\le\frac12\int|\xi_t|^2$ and $\int(F^TFv\cdot v+F^T(M^T-M)Fv\cdot z)\ge\frac12\int|\xi_t|^2$. This is the general theorem behind Lemma 4.1. It requires neither invertibility of $F$ nor a realization of $F$ as a particle-flow derivative. Here $Jw(t)=\int_0^tw(s)\,ds$.
notes.TorusEuler.paper_mean_inverse: Assume $0<T\le1$, smooth periodic coefficients $F,M$, $F_t=MF$, $F^{-1}$ bounded by $D\ge1$, $M$ bounded by $L\ge0$, and $-(M_t+M^2)\le I$. Let $K=F^TF$, $\Omega=F^T(M^T-M)F$, with nonnegative uniform bounds $K_0,K_1,\Omega_0,\Omega_1$ for these coefficients and their first label derivatives. Every continuous $C^{0,1/2}$ source then has a unique divergence-free endpoint velocity $v$ and constant field $c$, with $z(t)=\int_0^tv$ and $z(0)=z(T)=0$. The formal statement recovers a periodic zero-spatial-mean potential and bounds $v$ and the fixed-time projected inverse by $C(D+L+K_0+K_1+\Omega_0+\Omega_1)^{1164}$. The constant is chosen before the parent. The paper uses an unspecified exponent and larger $C^{1,1/2}$ coefficient norms. The $C^{0,1/2}$ norm takes the maximum of the supremum norm and half-Hölder seminorm.
notes.TorusEuler.paper_mean_inverse_smooth_for: Let $0<T\le1$, $D\ge1$, $L\ge0$. Suppose smooth periodic matrix fields satisfy $F_t=MF$, $G=F^{-1}$, $\|G\|\le D$, $\|M\|\le L$, and $-(M_t+M^2)\le I$. Every smooth periodic label force $f_{\mathrm{lab}}$ gives smooth periodic $z,v,B,\mathsf q$ with $z_t=v$, $z(0)=z(T)=0$, $\operatorname{div}_av=0$, $B=Fv$ and $B_t+MB+G^T\nabla_a\mathsf q=f_{\mathrm{lab}}$. The pressure has zero mean on the unit torus. To obtain the physical equation of Theorem 4.2 one must identify $F,M$ with the actual incompressible flow and set $f_{\mathrm{lab}}=f\circ X$.

Let $0<T\le1$, and let $U$ be smooth, periodic and divergence free with flow $X$. Assume $\|(D_aX)^{-1}\|\le D$, $D\ge1$, $\|D_xU\|\le L$, $L\ge0$, and $-(M_t+M^2)\le I$ along trajectories. For every smooth periodic force $f$, the formal statement constructs smooth periodic $b,q$ solving $b_t+(U\cdot
abla)b+(b\cdot
abla)U+
abla q=f$ and $\operatorname{div}b=0$. It first constructs label fields $z,v,B=Fv$ with $z_t=v$ and $z(0)=z(T)=0$, then sets $b=B\circ X^{-1}$. The label pressure has zero spatial mean. This is existence with the endpoint choice used in §1.2; uniqueness and a quantitative Hölder bound are not conclusions of this particular theorem.
notes.TorusEuler.paper_section_8_of_inductiveE: There is an initial-frequency threshold, chosen before the compatible approximate stages and central waves, above which they admit one finite positive accumulation time $T$ and one Euler limit $u,p$. Compatibility includes the prescribed schedule, smooth odd divergence-free periodic velocities, projected residual bounds, shrinking oscillation supports, small corrections and the central-wave crossing data. The conclusion gives uniform velocity convergence on $[0,T]$, convergence in every spatial Hölder order on each earlier interval, bounded velocity, central vorticity blow-up, maximality and both infinite integrals, and local $C^m$ limits for $u$ and $\partial_tu$ away from the torus origin. Every stage lasts beyond $T$ and $t_j\to T$. This theorem assumes the compatible stages and waves; it does not construct them from arbitrary initial data.
notes.TorusEuler.parentResidualFourierBand_of_: Let $U$ be a torus velocity whose lift is smooth on $[0,T]$, with $T>0$ and Fourier support in $|\xi|\le2\mathsf D$ for every time, where $\mathsf D\ge0$. At a fixed time, identify its advection with a half-Hölder torus field and suppose the within-interval time derivative equals $-\mathbb P(U\cdot\nabla U)+R_U$. Then $R_U$ has Fourier support in $|\xi|\le4\mathsf D$. Time differentiation preserves the velocity band, products add frequency supports, and the spatial projection preserves each frequency.
